terms.definition: Liability arising from extremely dangerous operations, such as blasting, that applies without exception for any resulting harm.
examples: The demolition firm's blasting cracked a neighbouring foundation, and absolute liability meant it owed for the damage even though every safety rule had been followed.

terms.definition: A clause in an insurance contract allowing the insurer to demand full payment under specific conditions such as non-payment or destruction of property.
examples: When the insured missed three months of payments, the acceleration clause let the insurer demand the full outstanding balance at once.

terms.definition: A workers' compensation claim in which the claims adjuster or administrator determines the worker's injury is covered.
examples: After reviewing the incident report and the medical file, the adjuster recorded it as an accepted claim, so the worker's treatment was covered.

terms.definition: An unforeseen, unintended event that causes bodily injury or property damage.
examples: A driver rear-ended her at a red light — an accident, since no one intended the collision or the damage that followed.

terms.definition: Coverage for medical, rehab, wage loss, and related costs after an auto injury.
examples: After the crash, his accident benefits paid for physiotherapy and replaced part of his lost wages while he was off work.

terms.definition: A discount preventing your insurance rate from increasing after your first at-fault accident.
examples: Because her policy included accident forgiveness, her premium stayed the same after she was found at fault for backing into a pole.

terms.definition: insurance for unforeseen bodily injury.
examples: The employer bought accident insurance for its warehouse crew so that a fall or a crush injury would be covered.

terms.definition: an insurance contract that provides coverage, singly or in combination, for death, dismemberment, disability, or hospital and medical care caused by or necessitated as a result of accident or specified kinds of accident.
examples: The travel plan was accident only, so it paid for the hospital stay after his ski fall but nothing for his flu.

terms.term: Accident Only or AD and D
terms.definition: policies providing coverage, singly or in combination, for death, dismemberment, disability, or hospital and medical care caused by or necessitated as a result of accident or specified kinds of accidents. Types of coverage include student accident, sports accident, travel accident, blanket accident, specific accident or accidental death and dismemberment (ADandD).
examples: The school's blanket accident-only plan covers students hurt at practice, paying set amounts for dismemberment or accidental death.
lookup_keys: accident only or ad and d

terms.definition: A police-generated document containing details of an auto accident used during claims processing.
examples: The adjuster asked for the accident report form so she could compare the officer's notes with the driver's own statement.

terms.definition: A category of loss summarizing the cause of loss, nature of the loss, or body part injured.
examples: Coding the accident type as "struck by falling object, shoulder" lets the safety team see which warehouse tasks cause the most injuries.

terms.definition: The twelve-month period used to measure the ultimate activity of all claims occurring during that period, regardless of when they were reported, opened, or closed.
examples: In accident year 2024 figures, a claim from a June 2024 crash counts there even though it was not reported until 2025.

terms.definition: unexpected injury to a person.
examples: Slipping on a wet floor and fracturing a wrist is an accidental bodily injury; a strain that built up over years is not.

terms.definition: an insurance contract that pays a stated benefit in the event of death and/or dismemberment caused by accident or specified kinds of accidents.
examples: His accidental death and dismemberment coverage paid a fixed sum when he lost a hand in the press, and would have paid more had he died.

terms.definition: Changing work duties or methods to permit a person to return to productive employment, including reasonable modifications to the work environment.
examples: As an accommodation, the employer moved the returning worker to a seated inspection role and raised his bench to avoid overhead reaching.

terms.definition: Coverage for the loss of records evidencing amounts owed, and the resulting inability to collect outstanding accounts receivable, due to a covered peril.
examples: Fire destroyed the billing records, and accounts receivable insurance covered the invoices the company could no longer prove or collect.

terms.definition: The vesting of a right in a party's favor.
examples: The right to interest on the unpaid settlement began to accrue the day the insurer's payment deadline passed.

terms.definition: period of time insured must incur eligible medical expenses at least equal to the deductible amount in order to establish a benefit period under a major medical expense or comprehensive medical expense policy.
examples: Her plan's accumulation period gave her six months to reach the deductible in eligible expenses before major medical benefits began.

terms.definition: Occupational medicine practice guidelines published by the American College of Occupational and Environmental Medicine.
examples: The examiner questioned the treatment plan because the ACOEM practice guidelines do not support an MRI in the first weeks of routine back pain.

terms.definition: An event resulting from natural causes without any human intervention.
examples: A hailstorm that shattered the skylights was an act of God, since nothing anyone did caused the storm.

terms.definition: repayment value for indemnification due to loss or damage of property; in most cases it is replacement cost minus depreciation
examples: The ten-year-old roof was settled at actual cash value, so the payout was replacement cost minus a decade of depreciation.

terms.definition: (PC Insurance) a document or other presentation, prepared as a formal means of conveying to the state regulatory authority and the Board of Directors, or its equivalent, the actuary's professional conclusions and recommendations, of recording and communicating the methods and procedures, of assuring that the parties addressed are aware of the significance of the actuary's opinion or findings and that documents the analysis underlying the opinion. (In Life and Health) this document would be called an "Actuarial Memorandum."
examples: The company's actuarial report set out its reserve methods and conclusions for the regulator and the board before the year-end filing.

terms.definition: business professional who analyzes probabilities of risk and risk management including calculation of premiums, dividends and other applicable insurance industry standards.
examples: The actuary reviewed five years of claims data and recommended a rate increase for young drivers in the region.

terms.definition: A person or entity, other than the named insured, protected against loss under an insurance policy or coverage document.
examples: The building owner was named an additional insured on the contractor's policy, so a passer-by's injury claim would fall to that policy.

terms.definition: Coverage for extra living costs when a home becomes uninhabitable.
examples: With the kitchen gone after the fire, additional living expense insurance paid for the family's hotel rooms and restaurant meals.

terms.definition: A party added to a policy with expanded rights and responsibilities.
examples: The newly acquired subsidiary was added as an additional named insured, giving it the right to report claims and receive notices directly.

terms.definition: a person who investigates claims and recommends settlement options based on estimates of damage and insurance policies held.
examples: The adjuster photographed the damage, checked the policy limits, and recommended settling the claim at $8,400.

terms.definition: A provider of services such as filings, coverage analysis, risk analysis, underwriting, policy issuance and control, loss control, and claims and litigation management.
examples: The city hired an administrator to issue policies, run loss control, and manage claims for its self-insured fleet.

terms.definition: hospital inpatient care for any medical condition.
examples: The plan required notice within 48 hours of any admission, so the hospital called the insurer the night he was brought in.

terms.definition: insurer assets which can be valued and included on the balance sheet to determine financial viability of the company.
examples: Office furniture is excluded from admitted assets, so it does not count toward the surplus regulators look at.

terms.definition: An insurance company licensed by a state's regulatory authority to do business in that state; also called an authorized company.
examples: Because the carrier is an admitted company in Texas, it files its rates with the state regulator and its policyholders have guaranty fund protection.

terms.definition: occur when a policy has been processed, and the premium has been paid prior to the effective date. These are a liability to the company and not included in written premium or the unearned premium reserve.
examples: The customer paid in November for a policy starting in January, so the money sat as advance premiums rather than written premium.

terms.definition: The tendency of poorer or less desirable risks to seek or continue insurance more than better risks do, and for insureds to exploit favorable options in their contracts.
examples: Offering generous flood coverage at one flat price invites adverse selection, since owners in the floodplain buy first and buy the most.

terms.definition: a group supported by member companies whose function is to gather loss statistics and publish trended loss costs.
examples: The insurer priced its new artisan contractor program using loss costs published by an advisory organization.

terms.definition: a person or entity that directly, or indirectly, through one or more other persons or entities, controls, is controlled by or is under common control with the insurer.
examples: The claims-handling firm is an affiliate of the insurer, since both are owned by the same holding company.

terms.definition: an individual who sells, services, or negotiates insurance policies either on behalf of a company or independently.
examples: The agent walked the shop owner through three quotes and bound the policy she chose that same afternoon.

terms.definition: the maximum dollar amount or total amount of coverage payable for a single loss, or multiple losses, during a policy period, or on a single project.
examples: The policy carried a $2 million aggregate, so once total payouts reached that figure nothing further would be paid that year.

terms.definition: A policy provision requiring the insured to maintain a stated or determinable amount of insurance.
examples: An aggregate amount clause required the warehouse owner to carry at least $5 million of insurance at all times.

terms.definition: method of reimbursement of a health plan with a corporate entity that directly provides care, where (1) the health plan is contractually required to pay the total operating costs of the corporate entity, less any income to the entity from other users of services, and (2) there are mutual unlimited guarantees of solvency between the entity and the health plan that put their respective capital and surplus at risk in guaranteeing each other.
examples: Under aggregate cost payments, the health plan reimburses the clinic group's full operating cost, less what other patients bring in.

terms.definition: Coverage under which the insured retains the full amount of losses, subject to its per-claim retention, until total retentions reach a specified dollar amount, after which the reinsurer pays the full amount of losses for the rest of the period.
examples: The district pays each claim up to its retention until losses total $3 million, after which aggregate excess coverage takes over.

terms.definition: The maximum amount of coverage an insurer or pool must pay for all losses during a specific period.
examples: Three separate lawsuits in one year exhausted the pool's aggregate limit, leaving the member to fund the fourth itself.

terms.definition: A physician agreed upon by the employer or third-party administrator and the employee or attorney to provide an opinion that may be considered final in a workers' compensation claim.
examples: Rather than argue over duelling reports, both sides chose an agreed medical examiner whose opinion settled the disability dispute.

terms.definition: coverage for aircraft (hull) and their contents; aircraft owners' and aircraft manufacturers liability to passengers, airports and other third parties.
examples: The aircraft line covers the hull itself plus the operator's liability to passengers and to the airport.

terms.definition: Coverage for the insured when negligent acts or omissions result in losses involving aircraft.
examples: When a mechanic's oversight caused a hard landing, aircraft insurance responded to the resulting damage and injury claims.

terms.definition: an insurance company formed according to the laws of a foreign country. The company must conform to state regulatory standards to legally sell insurance products in that state.
examples: A London-based insurer is an alien company in the United States and must meet each state's standards before selling there.

terms.definition: also known as open peril, this type of policy covers a broad range of losses. The policy covers risks not explicitly excluded in the policy contract.
examples: Her all risk policy covered the spilled paint that ruined the carpet, because spills were never listed as an exclusion.

terms.definition: Coverage for loss caused by all perils except those specifically excluded in the coverage document.
examples: Under all-risk insurance the adjuster looks for an exclusion first; if none applies, the loss is covered.

terms.definition: coverages which are generally written with property insurance, e.g., glass, tornado, windstorm and hail; sprinkler and water damage; explosion, riot, and civil commotion; growing crops; flood; rain; and damage from aircraft and vehicle, etc.
examples: Windstorm, sprinkler leakage, and flood are allied lines usually written alongside the building's fire coverage.

terms.definition: Expenses, such as court fees and outside legal counsel, that can be assigned directly to a particular claim.
examples: The $9,000 paid to defence counsel on that one file is allocated loss adjustment expense, unlike the claims department's general salaries.
The file carried an ALAE figure covering the outside counsel and expert fees tied to that single claim.

terms.definition: In lieu of vocational rehabilitation, a job for an injured or ill employee that accommodates the employee's permanent work limitations or restrictions.
examples: Instead of retraining, the employer offered alternate work at the parts counter, matching the doctor's twenty-pound lifting limit.

terms.definition: other than standard workers' compensation coverage, employer's liability and excess workers' compensation (e.g., large deductible, managed care).
examples: The chain used an alternative workers' compensation program with a large deductible and managed care rather than a standard policy.

terms.definition: health services provided to members who are not confined to a health care institution. Ambulatory services are often referred to as "outpatient" services.
examples: The knee scope was billed as ambulatory services because she went home the same afternoon.

terms.definition: A federal law prohibiting discrimination against disabled persons, requiring employers to afford disabled employees the same rights, opportunities, and benefits as other employees.
examples: The Americans with Disabilities Act required the employer to consider a modified schedule rather than terminate the employee outright.

terms.definition: an annual report required to be filed with each state in which an insurer does business. This report provides a snapshot of the financial condition of a company and significant events which occurred throughout the reporting year.
examples: The regulator compared this year's annual statement with last year's to see how reserves and surplus had moved.

terms.definition: the beneficiary of an annuity payment, or person during whose life and annuity is payable.
examples: Payments continue as long as the annuitant lives, and stop at her death unless a guarantee period applies.

terms.definition: an annuity contract that provides for the fixed payment of the annuity at the end of the first interval of payment after purchase. The interval may vary, however the annuity payouts must begin within 13 months.
examples: He bought an immediate non-variable annuity in March, and the first fixed monthly payment arrived in April.

terms.definition: a contract providing income for a specified period of time, or duration of life for a person or persons.
examples: She converted part of her savings into an annuity that pays a set amount every month for the rest of her life.

terms.definition: The legal recourse for reconsideration of a judgment or findings.
examples: After the judge denied the benefits, the worker filed an appeal asking a higher panel to reconsider the findings.

terms.definition: Under workers' compensation, the party, usually the injured worker, who establishes a case before a workers' compensation appeals board.
examples: The applicant, an injured forklift operator, opened his case by filing with the workers' compensation appeals board.

terms.definition: A questionnaire or survey providing information used to determine insurance coverage.
examples: The application asked about the roof's age, prior claims, and whether the building had a sprinkler system.

terms.definition: A form that, when filed, establishes a case before a workers' compensation appeals board and results in the assignment of a case number.
examples: Filing the Application for Adjudication of Claim opened the case and assigned it a number for the hearing.

terms.definition: A methodology for determining how much of an employee's permanent disability is due to an industrial injury versus other causes.
examples: Apportionment assigned sixty percent of the permanent disability to the workplace injury and forty percent to pre-existing arthritis.

terms.definition: An assessment of property value or damage performed by a qualified professional after a covered loss.
examples: The two sides were far apart on the fire loss, so an independent appraisal set the building's damage value.

terms.definition: An increase in the conversion value of property due to economic causes.
examples: The land's appreciation over fifteen years meant its market value far exceeded what the owner originally paid.

terms.definition: A process in which a third party appointed by two disputing parties considers the facts at issue and renders a binding, final decision.
examples: Rather than go to court, the two insurers went to arbitration, and the arbitrator's decision on fault was final for both.

terms.term: Arising Out of and Occurring in the Course of Employment (AOE/COE)
terms.definition: The requirement that an injury or illness be caused by, and occur during, a worker's job for it to be covered by workers' compensation.
examples: The strain met the AOE/COE test because it happened while he was loading a delivery truck during his shift.
lookup_keys: arising out of and occurring in the course of employment

terms.definition: Means you are behind on paying your insurance.
examples: Two missed instalments put the policy in arrears, and the insurer sent notice before cancelling it.

terms.definition: A person in custody whose release may be secured by posting bail.
examples: A bail bond let the arrestee leave custody while awaiting the hearing.

terms.definition: Intentional and malicious burning of property.
examples: Investigators ruled the warehouse fire arson after finding accelerant near the loading dock, and the claim was denied.

terms.definition: estimated value for real or personal property established by a taxing entity
examples: The town's assessed value for tax purposes was $310,000, well below what the house would fetch on the market.

terms.definition: in the risk-based capital formula, risk assigned to the company's assets.
examples: Holding a large block of lower-rated bonds raises the insurer's asset risk in the risk-based capital calculation.

terms.definition: probable future economic benefits obtained or controlled by a particular entity as a result of past transactions or events. An asset has three essential characteristics: It embodies a probable future benefit that involves a capacity, singly or in combination with other assets, to contribute directly or indirectly to future net cash inflows; A particular entity can obtain the benefit and control others' access to it; and The transaction or other event-giving rise to the entity's right to or control of the benefit has already occurred.
examples: Cash, bonds, and amounts recoverable from reinsurers are all assets, because each is expected to bring future economic benefit the company controls.

terms.definition: A governmental pool established to write business declined by carriers in the standard insurance market.
examples: After three at-fault crashes no carrier would quote him, so he was placed in the state's assigned risk pool.

terms.definition: a policy or rider that provides coverage only while a policyholder is confined to an assisted living facility and meets the policy requirements for coverage.
examples: The rider paid an assisted living care benefit each month she lived in the facility and needed help with daily activities.

terms.definition: the assumption of risk from another insurance entity within a reinsurance agreement or treaty.
examples: The reinsurer's assumed reinsurance grew after it took a share of two large property treaties.

terms.definition: Placing oneself in a position of known risk and danger.
examples: By stepping into the ring as a sparring partner, he accepted an assumption of risk for the bruises that followed.

terms.definition: The percentage of responsibility assigned to each driver involved in an accident.
examples: The insurers split it seventy-thirty, finding the turning driver mostly at fault.

terms.definition: A dangerous place or object attractive to children, requiring the owner to take unusual care to guard them from it.
examples: An unfenced backyard pool is a classic attractive nuisance, so the owner must fence and gate it against wandering children.

terms.definition: A survey of records to determine the premium or contribution owed for the protection furnished.
examples: The year-end audit of payroll records showed the contractor's exposure had grown, so an additional premium was billed.

terms.definition: an insurer licensed or admitted to do business in a particular state.
examples: Only an authorized company can issue this policy in the state; anything else would have to be written as surplus lines.

terms.term: Authorized Control Level Risk Based Capital
terms.definition: theoretical amount of capital plus surplus an insurance company should maintain.
examples: When the insurer's surplus fell below its authorized control level risk-based capital, the regulator gained power to step in.
lookup_keys: authorized control level risk based capital

terms.definition: reinsurance placed with a reinsurer who is licensed or otherwise allowed to conduct reinsurance within a state.
examples: Because the reinsurer is licensed in the state, the cession counts as authorized reinsurance and the ceding company takes full balance sheet credit.

terms.definition: coverage that protects against financial loss because of legal liability for motor vehicle related injuries (bodily injury and medical payments) or damage to the property of others caused by accidents arising out of ownership, maintenance or use of a motor vehicle (including recreational vehicles such as motor homes). Commercial is defined as all motor vehicle policies that include vehicles that are used primarily in connection with business, commercial establishments, activity, employment, or activities carried on for gain or profit. No Fault is defined by the state concerned.
examples: Auto liability paid the other driver's hospital bills and bumper repair after the company van ran a stop sign.

terms.definition: motor vehicle insurance coverage (including collision, vandalism, fire and theft) that insures against material damage to the insured's vehicle. Commercial is defined as all motor vehicle policies that include vehicles that are used in connection with business, commercial establishments, activity, employment, or activities carried on for gain or profit.
examples: Auto physical damage covered the hail dents on the fleet's pickups, even though no other vehicle was involved.

terms.definition: Insurance against loss of, or damage to, a vehicle from collision with another vehicle or object.
examples: Automobile collision insurance paid to repair her own bumper after she struck a guardrail.

terms.definition: Coverage on risks associated with driving or owning an automobile, including collision, liability, comprehensive, medical, and uninsured motorist coverages.
examples: His automobile insurance bundles liability, collision, comprehensive, and uninsured motorist coverage into one policy.

terms.definition: Insurance against bodily injury or property damage to others arising from accidents or use of a covered vehicle.
examples: Automobile liability insurance responded when he sideswiped a parked car and the owner claimed for the damage.

terms.definition: Optional coverage that pays medical expenses of passengers and insureds regardless of fault for the accident.
examples: Automobile medical payments insurance covered the passenger's emergency room visit before anyone had decided who caused the crash.

terms.definition: A medical examiner's report providing information on the cause of death.
examples: The life insurer requested the autopsy report to confirm whether the death was accidental.

terms.definition: The weekly amount prescribed by statute for disability or death benefits.
examples: State law set his average weekly benefits at two-thirds of his usual wage while he was off with a broken ankle.

terms.definition: Insurance protection against losses connected with airline or airplane accidents.
examples: Aviation insurance covered the charter operator's losses after a runway overrun damaged the aircraft and injured two passengers.

terms.definition: Eliminating hazards or exposures to prevent loss.
examples: Deciding not to store solvents on site at all is avoidance of risk, not merely reducing it.

terms.definition: Dishonest or misleading conduct in insurance dealings.
examples: Sitting on a clearly covered claim for eight months without explanation exposed the insurer to a bad faith suit.

terms.definition: One who has temporary possession of property belonging to another.
examples: The dry cleaner is a bailee for customers' garments and answers for them if a fire destroys the shop.

terms.definition: accounting statement showing the financial condition of a company at a particular date.
examples: The balance sheet showed exactly what the company owned and what it owed as of December 31.

terms.definition: A policy covering named perils only.
examples: The basic insurance policy listed fire, lightning, and explosion, so water damage from a burst pipe was not covered.

terms.definition: The limit of liability for which the basic rate on a liability coverage agreement is quoted.
examples: Rates are quoted at the basic limit of $100,000, with higher limits priced by applying an increased limits factor.

terms.definition: Building Code Effectiveness Grading Schedule - classification system for assessment of building codes per geographic region with special emphasis on mitigation of losses from natural disasters.
examples: A strong BCEGS grade for the municipality earned local property owners a small credit on their windstorm premiums.

terms.definition: an individual who may become eligible to receive payment due to will, life insurance policy, retirement plan, annuity, trust, or other contract.
examples: She named her sister the beneficiary, so the life policy pays her sister directly rather than passing through the estate.

terms.definition: Under workers' compensation, a payment made to a worker or dependent related to a compensable injury or condition.
examples: His weekly benefit began after the waiting period and continued until the doctor cleared him for full duty.

terms.definition: total expenditures for health care services paid to or on behalf of a member.
examples: The plan's benefits line totalled the year's payments to hospitals, clinics, and pharmacies on behalf of its members.

terms.definition: An enhancement of property value from improvements, as opposed to repairs or replacements.
examples: Replacing the worn shingles with a metal roof was betterment, so the insured paid the difference in value.

terms.definition: Guarantees a contractor will enter a contract and furnish required performance bonds.
examples: The city required a bid bond so that the low bidder could not simply walk away from the contract.

terms.definition: A temporary or preliminary agreement providing coverage until a policy can be written or delivered.
examples: The agent issued a binder that morning so the buyer could close on the house before the policy was printed.

terms.definition: A broad bond covering all employees.
examples: A blanket bond protected the credit union against theft by any employee, without naming individuals.

terms.definition: coverage for property and liability that extends to more than one location, class of property or employee.
examples: Blanket coverage let the retailer insure inventory across all twelve stores under a single limit.

terms.definition: Insurance covering more than one type of property at one location, or one or more types of property at several locations.
examples: Blanket insurance covered both the buildings and their contents at three warehouses under one amount.

terms.definition: Coverage for multiple items or locations under one total limit.
examples: Rather than list each excavator separately, the contractor wrote a blanket policy with one limit for the whole fleet.

terms.definition: Protection against loss caused by an organization's employees' dishonest acts.
examples: The blanket position bond paid out when a bookkeeper diverted company funds into a personal account.

terms.definition: covers damage to pleasure boats, motors, trailers, boating equipment and personal watercraft as well as bodily injury and property damage liability to others.
examples: The boatowners policy covered the cracked hull, the trailer, and the injury claim from a swimmer struck by the wake.

terms.definition: Any physical injury to a person; liability insurance covers bodily injury to a third party caused by an insured.
examples: The claim included bodily injury for the pedestrian's broken leg as well as damage to her bicycle.

terms.definition: Coverage that pays medical expenses for others injured in an accident you caused.
examples: Bodily injury liability paid the other driver's ambulance ride and surgery after our insured was found at fault.

terms.definition: Coverage for property damage resulting from accidents involving boilers, pressure vessels, chillers, or related property.
examples: When the hospital's chiller failed violently, boiler and machinery insurance covered the unit and the damaged room around it.

terms.term: Boiler and Machinery or Equipment Breakdown and Machinery
terms.definition: coverage for the failure of boilers, machinery and other electrical equipment. Benefits include (i) property of the insured, which has been directly damaged by the accident; (ii) costs of temporary repairs and expediting expenses; and (iii) liability for damage to the property of others. Coverage also includes inspection of the equipment.
examples: Equipment breakdown coverage paid for the burnt-out transformer, the rented temporary generator, and the neighbour's damaged wiring.
lookup_keys: boiler and machinery or equipment breakdown and machinery

terms.definition: An obligation of a surety to protect the obligee against financial loss caused by the act or omission of the principal.
examples: The surety issued a bond protecting the owner if the roofer failed to finish the job as promised.

terms.definition: a form of debt security whereby the debt holder has a creditor stake in the company. Obligations issued by business units, governmental units and certain nonprofit units having a fixed schedule for one or more future payments of money; includes commercial paper, negotiable certificates of deposit, repurchase agreements and equipment trust certificates.
examples: Most of the insurer's portfolio sits in bonds, which pay scheduled interest and return the principal at maturity.

terms.definition: original cost, including capitalized acquisition costs and accumulated depreciation, unamortized premium and discount, deferred origination and commitment fees, direct write-downs, and increase/decrease by adjustment.
examples: The building's book value is its original cost plus capitalized fees, less accumulated depreciation.

terms.definition: The passing of reinsurance from an insurer or pool to a reinsurer under a reinsurance contract.
examples: Each month the ceding insurer sent a bordereau listing every risk ceded and the premium attached to it.

terms.definition: Classification of a damaged vehicle as salvage, irreparable, rebuilt, or stolen.
examples: The insurer declared the flooded sedan a total loss, and the vehicle's title was branded salvage.

terms.definition: Failure to meet policy conditions or warranties.
examples: Leaving the alarm switched off was a breach of a policy warranty and gave the insurer grounds to deny the burglary claim.

terms.definition: an individual who receives commissions from the sale and service of insurance policies. These individuals work on behalf of the customer and are not restricted to selling policies for a specific company but commissions are paid by the company with which the sale was made.
examples: The broker shopped the account to five carriers and brought the two best quotes back to the client.

terms.definition: Insurance against loss to buildings and materials during construction; also known as course of construction coverage.
examples: Builder's risk covered the framing lumber and half-built walls when a storm flattened them mid-construction.

terms.definition: Coverage for property under construction.
examples: The developer carried builders risk insurance from groundbreaking until the building was handed over to the owner.

terms.definition: typically written on a reporting or completed value form, this coverage insures against loss to buildings in the course of construction. The coverage also includes machinery and equipment used in the course of construction and to materials incidental to construction.
examples: Written on a completed value form, the builders risk policy insured the structure, the on-site crane, and the stacked drywall.

terms.definition: Covers damage to company-owned buildings, such as fire, water damage, or damage to installations like electricity and heating.
examples: Building insurance paid to repair the office's scorched wiring and the water damage left behind by the fire crew.

terms.definition: Breaking and entering the premises of another with felonious intent.
examples: Forcing the back door open after hours to empty the tills was burglary, not simple theft.

terms.definition: coverage for property taken or destroyed by breaking and entering the insured's premises, burglary or theft, forgery or counterfeiting, fraud, kidnap and ransom, and off-premises exposure.
examples: Burglary and theft coverage responded when thieves cut through the roof and took $40,000 in electronics.

terms.definition: coverage for motor vehicles, other than those in the garage business, engaged in commerce. Business auto filings include singularly or in any combination coverage such as the following: Auto Liability, PIP, MP, Uninsured Motorist and/or Underinsured Motorists (UM/UIM); Specified Causes of Loss, Comprehensive, and Collision.
examples: The business auto policy covered the plumbing company's three vans for liability, collision, and uninsured motorists.

terms.definition: Various coverages protecting business operations and assets.
examples: Her business insurance covers the storefront, the stock inside it, and claims from customers who are hurt on the premises.

terms.definition: Protection for business owners against economic losses during a period when operations are interrupted.
examples: With the plant shut for six weeks, business interruption made up the profit the owner would otherwise have earned.

terms.definition: Business interruption insurance covers loss of income due to disruptions caused e.g. by fire or theft.
examples: Business interruption insurance replaced the restaurant's lost income during the two months it was closed for fire repairs.

terms.definition: Under workers' compensation or disability benefits, the hardship placed on a business that justifies releasing an employee due to injury or illness.
examples: The employer argued business necessity, since no available role fit the permanent restrictions on the injured worker.

terms.definition: business insurance typically for property, liability and business interruption coverage.
examples: A business owners policy gave the bakery property, liability, and business interruption coverage in a single package.

terms.definition: Explains how claims affected by local laws are handled.
examples: A by-law endorsement paid the extra cost of rebuilding to current code after the fire, including the sprinklers now required.

terms.definition: All claims activity, such as loss payments and claims opened or closed, occurring during a specific calendar year regardless of when the claim originated.
examples: Calendar year figures count every payment made during 2025, even on claims that occurred years earlier.

terms.definition: in health insurance, the amount that must be paid by the insured during a calendar year before the insurer becomes responsible for further loss costs.
examples: Her $1,500 calendar year deductible reset in January, so her out-of-pocket costs started over.

terms.definition: A California law similar to the federal Family Medical Leave Act that allows unpaid leave to care for a domestic partner and generally excludes pregnancy-related disabilities.
examples: The employee took unpaid leave under the California Family Rights Act to care for her domestic partner after surgery.

terms.definition: Requirements for immobilizer systems to prevent vehicle theft.
examples: The insurer offered a discount because the vehicle's immobilizer met the Canadian Theft Deterrent Standard.

terms.definition: Termination of insurance coverage during the policy period; flat cancellation ends coverage at the effective date without premium charge.
examples: The insurer processed a flat cancellation back to the effective date, so the customer paid nothing at all.

terms.definition: An insurer's ability to accept risk.
examples: After a heavy hurricane season the market's capacity shrank and carriers took on fewer coastal risks.

terms.definition: a company's assets minus its liabilities.
examples: The company's capital and surplus is simply what remains after subtracting its liabilities from its assets.

terms.definition: statutory requirement ordering companies to maintain their capital and surplus at an amount equal to or in excess of a specified amount to help assure the solvency of the company by providing a financial cushion against expected loss or misjudgments and generally measured as a company's admitted assets minus its liabilities, determined on a statutory accounting basis.
examples: Regulators would not license the new insurer until it met the state's capital and surplus requirement.

terms.definition: excess (deficiency) of the sales price of an asset over its book value. Calculated on the basis of original cost adjusted, as appropriate, for accrual of discount or amortization of premium and for depreciation.
examples: Selling the bond above its adjusted book value produced a capital gain for the quarter.

terms.definition: a compensation plan used in connection with some managed care contracts where a physician or other medical provider is paid a flat amount, usually on a monthly basis, for each subscriber who has elected to use that physician or medical provider. Capitated payments are sometimes expressed in terms of a "per member/per month" payment. The capitated provider is generally responsible, under the conditions of the contract, for delivering or arranging for the delivery of all contracted health services required by the covered person.
examples: Under the capitation arrangement the clinic receives a set amount per member each month, whether or not that patient books an appointment.

terms.definition: an individual who sells or services insurance contracts for a specific insurer or fleet of insurers.
examples: As a captive agent she can only place business with the one insurer whose name is on her office door.

terms.definition: An insurer owned and controlled by its policyholders.
examples: The trucking firms formed a captive insurance company so that the businesses buying the coverage also owned the insurer.

terms.definition: an insurance company established by a parent firm for the purpose of insuring the parent's exposures.
examples: Rather than buy cover on the open market, the retailer set up a captive insurer to write its own property risks.

terms.definition: A liability exclusion denying coverage for damage to others' property that is in the insured's care, custody, or control.
examples: The care, custody and control exclusion meant the mechanic's liability policy would not pay for the customer's car he damaged on the hoist.

terms.definition: the SAP book value plus accrued interest and reduced by any valuation allowance and any nonadmitted adjustment applied to the individual investment.
examples: The bond's carrying value is its statutory book value plus accrued interest, less any valuation allowance.

terms.definition: A document from defense counsel, provided within 30 days of assignment, assessing the merits of a case, available defenses, and a recommended budget.
examples: Defence counsel filed a case evaluation and plan within thirty days, setting out the available defences and a budget for the file.

terms.definition: Reserves established for individual claims, which may be modified over time as new facts become known.
examples: The adjuster raised the case reserves from $15,000 to $60,000 once surgery was recommended.

terms.definition: a medium of exchange.
examples: The insurer keeps enough cash on hand to pay claims without having to sell investments.

terms.definition: short-term, highly liquid investments that are both (a) readily convertible to known amounts of cash, and (b) so near their maturity that they present insignificant risk of changes in value because of changes in interest rates. Investments with original maturities of three months or less qualify under this definition.
examples: A 90-day treasury bill counts as a cash equivalent because it converts to a known amount of cash almost immediately.

terms.definition: amount due to the policyholder upon surrender of the insurance or annuity product
examples: She surrendered the policy after twenty years and received its cash value rather than a death benefit.

terms.definition: A person who has been injured and is entitled to compensation.
examples: The report listed one casualty, the passenger who was hurt and entitled to compensation.

terms.definition: a form of liability insurance providing coverage for negligent acts and omissions such as workers compensation, errors and omissions, fidelity, crime, glass, boiler, and various malpractice coverages.
examples: Casualty insurance covers the firm's negligence exposures, from workers compensation to errors and omissions and crime.

terms.definition: A sudden and severe disaster causing an extraordinarily large loss.
examples: The wildfire was a catastrophe, destroying hundreds of homes and generating thousands of claims in a single week.

terms.definition: Bonds issued by an insurance company with funding tied to the company's losses from disasters, or acts of God. A loss exceeding a certain size triggers a reduction in the bond value or a change in the bond structure as loss payments are paid out of bond funds.
examples: The insurer issued catastrophe bonds so that investors, not the balance sheet, would absorb losses beyond a set hurricane threshold.

terms.definition: a large magnitude loss with little ability to forecast.
examples: A single earthquake produced a catastrophe loss far larger than anything the pricing model had anticipated.

terms.definition: A computer-based process simulating catastrophic events to estimate financial loss, including insured loss.
examples: The catastrophe model simulated ten thousand hurricane seasons to estimate what the insurer's coastal book might lose in a bad year.

terms.definition: Under workers' compensation, the legal determination that employment caused an illness or injury.
examples: Causation was disputed because the worker's shoulder pain could have come from a weekend hockey game rather than the job.

terms.definition: The basis upon which a suit may be brought against another party.
examples: Negligent maintenance of the stairwell gave the injured tenant a cause of action against the landlord.

terms.definition: To purchase reinsurance.
examples: The insurer chose to cede half the risk on the refinery account rather than hold it alone.

terms.definition: amount of premium (fees) used to purchase reinsurance.
examples: Ceded premium rose sharply this year because the company bought more reinsurance protection for its property book.

terms.definition: an insurance company that transfers risk by purchasing reinsurance.
examples: As ceding company, the insurer keeps handling the policy and the claims but passes part of the risk to its reinsurer.

terms.definition: An insurer or pool that places reinsurance of its original risk with a reinsurance company.
examples: The ceding insurance pool placed reinsurance on its largest school buildings before the storm season began.

terms.definition: Evidence that a specific entity or property is covered by insurance.
examples: The general contractor would not let the crew on site until each subcontractor produced a certificate of insurance.

terms.definition: a change in the interest rate, mortality assumption or reserving method or other factors affecting the reserve computation of policies in force.
examples: Moving to a newer mortality table was a change in valuation basis and required disclosure in the annual statement.

terms.definition: RESPA prohibits sellers from requiring a specific title insurer.
examples: Under the choice of title insurer rule, the seller could recommend a title company but could not require one.

terms.definition: A demand for payment of damages under a coverage agreement, insurance contract, or bond, or notice of an event that may have caused such damage.
examples: The homeowner filed a claim the morning after the pipe burst, demanding payment for the ruined flooring.

terms.definition: The act of assigning a claim or lawsuit for adjusting.
examples: The claim assignment sent the file to an adjuster who specialises in commercial fire losses.

terms.definition: A demand for compensation due to a loss.
examples: He submitted a claim for compensation for the tools stolen from his locked van.

terms.definition: Under workers' compensation, a form used to report a work injury or illness to the employer.
examples: The employee filled out a claim form and gave it to her supervisor the day after she hurt her back.

terms.definition: The rate of claims or accidents and a measure of their seriousness, respectively.
examples: Claim frequency fell after the new guards were installed, though claim severity rose because the remaining injuries were serious ones.

terms.definition: The funds set aside to cover all reported and reserved claims, including claim adjustment expenses and a reserve for incurred but not reported claims.
examples: The claim liability on the balance sheet covers reported claims, adjustment expenses, and an estimate for losses not yet reported.

terms.definition: A person who submits a claim for benefits under an insurance policy.
examples: The claimant submitted receipts and photographs to support her request for payment under the policy.

terms.definition: The insurance representative who investigates a claim and determines the settlement amount.
examples: The claims adjuster inspected the roof, spoke to the contractor, and set the settlement at $22,000.

terms.definition: costs expected to be incurred in connection with the adjustment and recording of accident and health, auto medical and workers' compensation claims.
examples: Claims adjustment expenses include the medical bill review and the examiner's time spent on each health file.

terms.definition: A person or group that adjusts workers' compensation claims for employers; also called a claims examiner, claims adjuster, or third-party administrator.
examples: The claims administrator handling the county's workers' compensation files approved the physiotherapy referral.

terms.definition: An employee overseeing adjusters and approving settlements.
examples: The claims examiner reviewed the adjuster's report and signed off on the settlement, which exceeded the adjuster's own authority.

terms.definition: Coverage that responds to claims brought during the policy period, regardless of when the loss occurred.
examples: Under claims made insurance the 2019 error is covered because the lawsuit landed while the current policy was in force.

terms.definition: A type of liability insurance form that only pays if the both event that causes (triggers)the claim and the actual claim are submitted to the insurance company during the policy term
examples: On a claims-made form the incident and the claim must both fall inside the policy term for the insurer to pay.

terms.definition: Coverage triggered when a claim is filed, regardless of event date.
examples: Their claims-made policy responded to the malpractice suit filed this year over treatment given three years ago.

terms.definition: a method of determining rates for all applicants within a given set of characteristics such as personal demographic and geographic location.
examples: Class rating put both drivers in the same band because they share an age group, a postal code, and a vehicle type.

terms.definition: Policy wording describing limits or modifications.
examples: The cancellation clause spells out how many days' notice each side must give.

terms.definition: A rating system using claims data to classify vehicle insurance risk.
examples: The CLEAR system uses real claims history to rank how expensive each vehicle model is to insure.

terms.definition: A claim for which no further action is expected and which is not being actively adjudicated for any benefits or appeals.
examples: The file was marked a closed claim once the settlement cleared and the appeal window passed.

terms.definition: Requires carrying a minimum amount of insurance to receive full coverage.
examples: The co-insurance clause required insurance equal to eighty percent of the building's value, and falling short cut the payout.

terms.definition: Companies sharing the same risk.
examples: Two carriers acted as co-insurers on the stadium, each taking half of the risk and half of the premium.

terms.definition: A fixed amount an insured must pay for a covered service, usually at the time of service.
examples: Her plan charges a $30 co-payment for each specialist visit, collected at the front desk.

terms.definition: A clause contained in most property insurance policies to encourage policy holders to carry a reasonable amount of insurance. If the insured fails to maintain the amount specified in the clause (Usually at least 80%), the insured shares a higher proportion of the loss. In medical insurance a percentage of each claim that the insured will bear.
examples: Because the owner insured the warehouse for only half its value, coinsurance meant he absorbed a share of the fire loss himself.

terms.definition: Falling in of a building.
examples: The claim was denied because the sagging floor had not yet met the policy's definition of collapse.

terms.definition: an agreement to receive payments as the buyer of an Option, Cap or Floor and to make payments as the seller of a different Option, Cap or Floor.
examples: The treasurer used a collar, buying a cap and selling a floor, to keep borrowing costs inside a set range.

terms.definition: unconditional obligations for the payment of money secured by the pledge of an investment.
examples: The collateral loan was secured by a pledge of the borrower's bond portfolio.

terms.definition: an investment-grade bond backed by a pool of low-grade debt securities, such as junk bonds, separated into tranches based on various levels of credit risk.
examples: Collateralized bond obligations bundle low-grade debt and slice it into tranches carrying different levels of credit risk.

terms.definition: a type of mortgage-backed security (MBS) with separate pools of pass-through security mortgages that contain varying classes of holders and maturities (tranches) with the advantage of predictable cash flow patterns.
examples: Collateralized mortgage obligations divide the pool's payments into tranches so investors can choose a maturity that suits them.

terms.definition: A written agreement between an employer and a union setting out the terms, conditions, rights, and duties governing work.
examples: The collective bargaining agreement set out shift premiums, seniority rules, and the grievance process.

terms.definition: Impact between moving objects or with fixed objects.
examples: The claim was coded a collision because the van struck a lamp post.

terms.definition: Reimburses for damage to your automobile from collision with another car or object.
examples: Collision coverage paid to fix his own car after he hit a concrete barrier.

terms.definition: Coverage that pays to repair or replace your vehicle after a collision.
examples: Her collision coverage replaced the vehicle outright when repairs would have cost more than it was worth.

terms.definition: Waives your collision deductible if hit by a negligent uninsured motorist.
examples: Because the at-fault driver had no insurance, the collision deductible waiver meant she paid nothing out of pocket.

terms.definition: Coverage against loss to insured property caused by striking or being struck by an object, including vehicle upset.
examples: Collision insurance also applies when the vehicle rolls over, not just when it strikes something.

terms.definition: Coverage for collision or rollover damage.
examples: Collision or upset insurance covered the tractor that tipped into a ditch on the farm road.

terms.definition: a special form of package policy composed of personal automobile and homeowners insurance.
examples: The combination policy put the family's home and both cars under one contract with a single renewal date.

terms.definition: an indication of the profitability of an insurance company, calculated by adding the loss and expense ratios.
examples: A combined ratio of 97 means the insurer paid out and spent less than it took in as premium.

terms.definition: date when the organization first became obligated for any insurance risk via the issuance of policies and/or entering into a reinsurance agreement. Same as "effective date" of coverage.
examples: The commencement date on the certificate is January 1, the day the insurer first took on the risk.

terms.definition: coverage for motor vehicles owned by a business engaged in commerce that protects the insured against financial loss because of legal liability for motor vehicle related injuries, or damage to the property of others caused by accidents arising out of the ownership, maintenance, use, or care-custody and control of a motor vehicle. This includes Commercial Auto Combinations of Business Auto, Garage, Truckers and/or Other Commercial Auto.
examples: Commercial auto covered the delivery fleet, the tow trucks, and the vehicles kept at the garage.

terms.definition: Vehicles used for business purposes.
examples: The pickup is a commercial automobile because it hauls tools and materials to job sites all week.

terms.definition: earthquake property coverage for commercial ventures.
examples: The bottling plant bought commercial earthquake coverage after a fault line was mapped nearby.

terms.definition: a commercial package policy for farming and ranching risks that includes both property and liability coverage. Coverage includes barns, stables, other farm structures and farm inland marine, such as mobile equipment and livestock.
examples: The commercial farm and ranch policy insured the barns, the mobile irrigation equipment, and the herd.

terms.definition: separate flood insurance policy sold to commercial ventures.
examples: The distribution centre sat outside the levee, so the owner bought a separate commercial flood policy.

terms.definition: flexible and broad commercial liability coverage with two major sub-lines: premises/operations sub-line and products/completed operations sub-line.
examples: Commercial general liability responded to both a customer's fall in the aisle and a defect in a product sold last year.

terms.definition: Coverage for alcohol-related liability of establishments.
examples: Commercial host liability covered the bar after a patron who had been overserved caused a crash.

terms.definition: Protects a business against claims if a customer or third party is harmed by the company's products, services, or activities.
examples: Commercial liability insurance paid the claim when a customer was scalded by a faulty coffee machine the company had installed.

terms.definition: a type of mortgage-backed security that is secured by the loan on a commercial property.
examples: The bonds were commercial mortgage-backed securities, secured by loans on shopping centres and office towers.

terms.definition: policy that packages two or more insurance coverages protecting an enterprise from various property and liability risk exposures. Frequently includes fire, allied lines, various other coverages (e.g., difference in conditions) and liability coverage. Such coverages would be included in other annual statement lines, if written individually. Include under this type of insurance multi-peril policies (other than farmowners, homeowners and automobile policies) that include coverage for liability other than auto.
examples: The commercial multiple peril policy bundled fire, allied lines, and liability coverage for the manufacturer into one contract.

terms.definition: provides a broad package of property and liability coverages for commercial ventures other than those provided insurance through a business owners policy.
examples: The commercial package policy let the mid-sized manufacturer pick property, liability, and crime coverages in one contract.

terms.definition: property insurance coverage sold to commercial ventures.
examples: Commercial property insured the building shell, the machinery bolted inside, and the stock on the shelves.

terms.definition: Coverage for portable commercial property.
examples: A commercial property floater followed the surveyor's instruments from site to site rather than covering one address.

terms.definition: All-risk coverage for commercial stock and property.
examples: The commercial property policy paid for the ruined stock because the cause of loss was not excluded anywhere in the wording.

terms.definition: a percentage of premium paid to agents by insurance companies for the sale of policies.
examples: The agent earned a fifteen percent commission on the premium for the policies she placed that month.

terms.definition: Coverage for transportation firms that must carry any customer's goods if paid.
examples: Common carrier liability applies to the freight line, which must accept any paying customer's goods and answer for damage to them.

terms.definition: a rating system where standard rating is established and usually adjusted within specific guidelines for each group on the basis of anticipated utilization by the group's employees.
examples: Under community rating everyone in the group pays the same base rate, adjusted only within set guidelines.

terms.definition: a five-digit identifying number assigned by NAIC, assigned to all insurance companies filing financial data with NAIC.
examples: Analysts pull filings by company code rather than by name, since several insurers share similar names.

terms.definition: Under workers' compensation, a term commonly used to refer to benefits paid to employees by employers or insurers.
examples: His compensation included wage replacement and payment of every approved medical bill.

terms.definition: Liability insurance covering accidents arising from past operations that have been completed or abandoned.
examples: Completed operations covered the electrician when a panel he had wired two years earlier caught fire.

terms.definition: policies covering the liability of contractors, plumbers, electricians, repair shops, and similar firms to persons who have incurred bodily injury or property damage from defective work or operations completed or abandoned by or for the insured, away from the insured's premises.
examples: Completed operations liability answers for the plumber whose finished work floods a customer's basement months later.

terms.definition: Coverage for direct and accidental loss or damage to your automobile, including fire, theft, or malicious mischief.
examples: Comprehensive covered the shattered windshield and the tree branch that dented the hood during the storm.

terms.definition: line of business providing for medical coverages; includes hospital, surgical, major medical coverages; does not include Medicare Supplement, administrative services (ASC) contracts, administrative services only (ASO) contracts, federal employees health benefit plans (FEHBP), medical only programs, Medicare and Medicaid programs, vision only and dental only business.
examples: The comprehensive hospital and medical line reports the plan's ordinary hospital, surgical, and major medical business.

terms.definition: Coverage for non-collision damage like fire, theft, or vandalism.
examples: Comprehensive auto coverage paid out when the car was stolen from the driveway overnight.

terms.definition: Insurance against physical loss to a vehicle other than collision.
examples: Comprehensive automobile insurance answers for fire, theft, and vandalism, while collision handles impacts.

terms.definition: Coverage for non-collision damage such as theft, fire, vandalism, or falling objects.
examples: Comprehensive coverage paid for the deer strike and the hail damage, neither of which counts as a collision.

terms.definition: coverage of all business liabilities unless specifically excluded in the policy contract.
examples: Comprehensive general liability covers the business against anything not written into the exclusions.

terms.definition: All-risk coverage for glass breakage, excluding war and fire.
examples: Comprehensive glass insurance paid to replace the storefront window after a stone shattered it.

terms.definition: comprehensive liability coverage for exposures arising out of the residence premises and activities of individuals and family members. (Non-business liability exposure protection for individuals.)
examples: Comprehensive personal liability covered the homeowner when his dog bit a visitor in the driveway.

terms.definition: policies that provide fully insured indemnity, HMO, PPO, or Fee for Service coverage for hospital, medical, and surgical expenses. Coverage excludes Short-Term Medical Insurance, the Federal Employees Health Benefit Program and non-comprehensive coverage such as basic hospital only, medical only, hospital confinement indemnity, surgical, outpatient indemnity, specified disease, intensive care, and organ and tissue transplant coverage.
examples: The employer's comprehensive medical plan covers hospital stays, doctor visits, and surgery, unlike a specified disease policy.

terms.definition: A final settlement of a workers' compensation case in which the parties agree on a lump-sum payment, usually settling all outstanding issues except future vocational rehabilitation.
examples: The parties signed a compromise and release, closing the claim with a single lump-sum payment.

terms.definition: property loss incurred from two or more perils in which only one loss is covered but both are paid by the insurer due to simultaneous incident.
examples: Concurrent causation applied because wind and flood struck together and the insurer paid the whole loss.

terms.definition: The legal taking of private property for public use.
examples: The highway widening led to condemnation of a strip of the farmer's front field.

terms.definition: A report describing the current state of a building or item, used for insurance assessment.
examples: The surveyor's condition report noted the aging roof and cracked masonry before the policy was issued.

terms.definition: requirements specified in the insurance contract that must be upheld by the insured to qualify for indemnification.
examples: Policy conditions required the insured to report theft to police within 24 hours and to keep the damaged goods for inspection.

terms.definition: Ownership of a unit plus shared property interest.
examples: Buying a condominium gave her title to the unit itself and a shared interest in the lobby, roof, and grounds.

terms.definition: homeowners insurance sold to condominium owners occupying the described property.
examples: Her condo policy covered the interior finishes and belongings, while the corporation's policy handled the building envelope.

terms.definition: Damage or loss not directly caused by damage to property but arising as a result of it.
examples: The freezer survived the fire, but the spoiled food inside was a consequential loss.

terms.definition: covering the liability of an insured to persons who have incurred bodily injury or property damage from alterations involving demolition, new construction or change in size of a structure on the insured's premises.
examples: Construction and alteration liability responded when demolition next door cracked a neighbour's wall.

terms.definition: A loss sufficient in amount that the cost of salvaging or repairing the property equals or exceeds its repaired value.
examples: The insurer declared a constructive total loss because repairing the flooded car would have cost more than the car was worth.

terms.definition: Under California workers' compensation, a permanent disability rating provided by the Disability Evaluation Unit when a claim is litigated or the injured worker is represented by an attorney.
examples: Because the worker had retained a lawyer, the Disability Evaluation Unit issued a consultative rating on the permanent disability.

terms.definition: required by some jurisdictions as a hedge against adverse experience from operations, particularly adverse claim experience.
examples: The regulator required contingency reserves so the plan could absorb an unusually bad run of claims.

terms.definition: the liability of an insured to persons who have incurred bodily injury or property damage from work done by an independent contractor hired by the insured to perform work that was illegal, inherently dangerous, or directly supervised by the insured
examples: Contingent liability attached to the owner because the excavation work he closely supervised was inherently dangerous.

terms.definition: statutory or contractual provision requiring providers to deliver care to an enrollee for some period following the date of a Health Plan Company's insolvency.
examples: A continuation of care requirement kept the clinic treating enrolled patients for ninety days after the plan became insolvent.

terms.definition: senior housing arrangements that in addition to housing include some provision for skilled nursing care.
examples: The continuing care retirement community offers independent apartments now and skilled nursing later, on the same campus.

terms.definition: A legally enforceable agreement.
examples: An insurance policy is a contract, so both the insurer and the insured can be held to its terms.

terms.definition: An insurance contract or coverage document offering limited bargaining between the parties.
examples: Because the policy is a contract of adhesion the customer could not negotiate its wording, so ambiguities are read in her favour.

terms.definition: reserves set up when, due to the gross premium structure, the future benefits exceed the future net premium. Contract reserves are in addition to claim and premium reserves.
examples: Contract reserves are held when future benefits promised on the policy exceed the future net premiums coming in.

terms.definition: A tort liability demand or complaint arising from an alleged breach of contract or agreement.
examples: The supplier's failure to deliver on time led to a contract tort liability claim from the builder.

terms.definition: liability coverage of an insured who has assumed the legal liability of another party by written or oral contract. Includes a contractual liability policy providing coverage for all obligations and liabilities incurred by a service contract provider under the terms of service contracts issued by the provider.
examples: Contractual liability coverage applied because the tenant had agreed in the lease to answer for the landlord's exposure.

terms.definition: Term life insurance that can be converted into permanent insurance without a medical exam.
examples: Her convertible term policy let her move to permanent coverage at forty without another medical exam.

terms.definition: an insurance policy that can be converted into permanent insurance without a medical assessment. The insurer is required to renew the policy regardless of the health of the insured subject to policy conditions.
examples: He exercised the convertible term insurance option after a diagnosis, and the insurer had to issue the permanent policy anyway.

terms.definition: provision to eliminate over insurance and establish a prompt and orderly claims payment system when a person is covered by more than one group insurance and/or group service plan.
examples: Coordination of benefits made her employer's plan pay first and her spouse's plan cover part of the remainder.

terms.definition: a cost sharing mechanism in group insurance plans where the insured pays a specified dollar amount of incurred medical expenses and the insurer pays the remainder.
examples: The plan's $20 copay applies at each visit, and the insurer pays whatever the appointment costs beyond that.

terms.definition: commissioner's directive of action to be completed by an insurer.
examples: The commissioner issued a corrective order requiring the insurer to fix its claims handling within ninety days.

terms.definition: The amount of loss that must be paid by an insured or pool before a reinsurance contract affords coverage.
examples: The pool absorbs the first $500,000 of losses as a corridor deductible before the reinsurance contract responds.

terms.definition: An analysis of the total cost of adjusting or litigating a claim versus its likely settlement or trial value.
examples: A cost/benefit analysis showed that fighting the $40,000 claim would cost more in legal fees than settling it.

terms.definition: Bonds required of litigants to pursue certain court remedies.
examples: The plaintiff posted a court bond before the judge would grant the injunction.

terms.definition: The protection and benefits provided by an insurance policy.
examples: The homeowner assumed she had coverage for sewer backup, but that protection was not in her policy.

terms.definition: The total number of lives insured, including dependents, under individual policies and group certificates.
examples: The plan reported 42,000 covered lives, counting employees and their dependents together.

terms.definition: Accidents or damages that are included in your insurance policy's protection.
examples: A kitchen fire is a covered loss under her policy; ordinary wear on the cabinets is not.

terms.definition: The measure of relative weight given to a body of loss experience data for actuarial analysis; credibility generally increases as the body of experience becomes more extensive.
examples: Ten years of data from a large fleet has high credibility, so the actuary weighted it heavily in the rate.

terms.definition: individual or group policies that provide benefits to a debtor for full or partial repayment of debt associated with a specific loan or other credit transaction upon disability or involuntary unemployment of debtor, except in connection with first mortgage loans.
examples: Credit insurance made his loan payments during the months he was out of work after the injury.

terms.term: Credit Accident and Health (group and individual)
terms.definition: coverage provided to or offered to borrowers in connection with a consumer credit transaction where the proceeds are used to repay a debt or an installment loan in the event the consumer is disabled as the result of an accident, including business not exceeding 120 months duration.
examples: Credit accident and health coverage kept up the car loan payments while the borrower recovered from an accident.

terms.definition: an insurance certificate issued on an existing insurance contract indicating that another insurer has assumed all of the risk under the contract from the ceding insurance company.
examples: A credit assumption agreement told the policyholder that a new insurer had taken over all risk under her existing contract.

terms.definition: coverage purchased by manufacturers, merchants, educational institutions, or other providers of goods and services extending credit, for indemnification of losses or damages resulting from the nonpayment of debts owed to them for goods or services provided in the normal course of their business.
examples: The equipment supplier bought credit default coverage in case a large customer failed to pay for goods delivered.

terms.definition: makes monthly loan/credit transaction payments to the creditor upon the disablement of an insured debtor.
examples: Credit disability coverage paid the monthly instalments directly to the lender while the borrower was unable to work.

terms.definition: policy assigning creditor as beneficiary for insurance on a debtor thereby remitting balance of payment to creditor should the debtor become disabled.
examples: Under credit health insurance the lender is the beneficiary, so the balance is paid down if the borrower becomes disabled.

terms.definition: credit insurance that provides a monthly or lump sum benefit during an unpaid leave of absence from employment resulting from specified causes, such as layoff, business closure, strike, illness of a close relative and adoption or birth of a child. This insurance is sometimes referred to as Credit Family Leave.
examples: Credit involuntary unemployment coverage paid her loan instalments during the three months the plant was closed.

terms.definition: makes loan/credit transaction payments to the creditor when the debtor becomes involuntarily unemployed.
examples: The benefit went straight to the creditor once the layoff triggered the credit involuntary unemployment coverage.

terms.definition: policy assigning creditor as beneficiary for insurance on a debtor thereby remitting balance of payment to creditor upon death of debtor.
examples: Credit life insurance paid off the remaining car loan when the borrower died, leaving nothing for the family to settle.

terms.definition: insurance written in connection with a credit transaction where the collateral is not a motor vehicle, mobile home or real estate and that covers perils to the goods purchased through a credit transaction or used as collateral for a credit transaction and that concerns a creditor's interest in the purchased goods or pledged collateral, either in whole or in part; or covers perils to goods purchased in connection with an open-end transaction.
examples: The store arranged credit personal property insurance on the financed furniture, protecting the lender's interest in the goods.

terms.definition: insurance that is purchased unilaterally by the creditor, who is the named insured, subsequent to the date of the credit transaction, providing coverage against loss, expense or damage to property as a result of fire, theft, collision or other risks of loss that would either impair a creditor's interest or adversely affect the value of collateral. "Creditor Placed Home" means "Creditor Placed Insurance" on homes, mobile homes and other real estate. "Creditor Placed Auto" means insurance on automobiles, boats or other vehicles.
examples: When the borrower let the policy lapse, the lender bought credit placed insurance on the house and added the cost to the loan.

terms.definition: part of the risk-based capital formula that addresses the collectability of a company's receivables and the risk of losing a provider or intermediary that has received advance capitation payments.
examples: Credit risk in the formula reflects the chance that reinsurers or providers fail to pay what they owe the company.

terms.definition: single interest or dual interest credit insurance that is purchased unilaterally by the creditor, who is the named insured, subsequent to the date of the credit transaction, providing coverage against loss to property that would either impair a creditor's interest or adversely affect the value of collateral on automobiles, boats, or other vehicles.
examples: After the borrower's auto policy lapsed, the lender bought creditor placed auto coverage to protect its interest in the vehicle.

terms.definition: single interest or dual interest credit insurance purchased unilaterally by the creditor, who is the named insured, subsequent to the date of the credit transaction, providing coverage against loss to property that would either impair a creditor's interest or adversely affect the value of collateral on homes, mobile homes, and other real estate.
examples: Creditor placed home coverage was added to the mortgage when the owner's own house insurance was cancelled.

terms.definition: Program assisting police through anonymous crime tips.
examples: A Crime Stoppers tip led police to the ring staging the staged collisions the insurer had flagged.
