terms.definition: Health insurance providing income payments when income is interrupted due to illness or accident.

terms.definition: A factor applied to outstanding losses to estimate their present value at a specified interest rate.

terms.definition: Premium discount for completing approved training.

terms.definition: Coverage against loss caused by earthquake.

terms.definition: coverage to protect against losses arising out of damage to or destruction of electronic data processing equipment and its software.

terms.definition: The date an insurance policy or coverage comes into effect and protection begins.

terms.definition: liability coverage for bodily injury or property damage arising from the use of elevators or escalators operated, maintained or controlled by the insured.

terms.definition: A claim that meets the insurance company's requirements and is therefore eligible for compensation.

terms.definition: Items used on a machine or vehicle.

examples: Joint and several liability let the plaintiff collect the full judgment from either defendant.

terms.definition: a loss-sharing mechanism combining several insurance companies to provide extra capacity due to type or size of exposure.
examples: The carriers formed a joint underwriting association to provide capacity for coastal properties no single insurer would take alone.

terms.definition: an annuity contract that ceases upon the death of the first of two or more annuitants.
examples: The joint-life annuity stopped when the first of the two annuitants died.

terms.definition: Bond required in civil and criminal court actions.
examples: The court required a judicial bond before the appeal could proceed.

terms.definition: a policy purchased by, for the benefit of, a business insuring the life or lives of personnel integral to the business operations.
examples: Key-persons insurance paid the firm a lump sum when its lead engineer died unexpectedly.

terms.definition: coverage for ransom or extortion costs and related expenses.
examples: Kidnap and ransom insurance covered the ransom, the negotiator's fees, and the travel costs during the incident.

terms.definition: termination of a policy due to failure to pay the required renewal premium.
examples: The policy lapsed when the renewal premium went unpaid past the grace period.

terms.definition: The theory of probability that, the larger the number of risks, the more closely actual results will approach probable expected results.
examples: The law of large numbers is why an insurer with 200,000 auto policies can predict its yearly claims far better than one with 200.

terms.definition: Prepaid legal coverage sold on a group basis.
examples: The union's legal insurance plan gave members prepaid access to a lawyer for wills and landlord disputes.

terms.definition: Obligation to pay for harm caused.
examples: The court found the driver had legal liability for the pedestrian's injuries and ordered him to pay.

terms.definition: Title insurance protecting the lender against claims on the property.
examples: The bank required a lender's policy so its mortgage interest would be protected against any title defect.

terms.definition: life insurance policy for which the cost is equally distributed over the term of the premium period, remaining constant throughout.
examples: Under level premium insurance the payment stays at $85 a month for the whole twenty-year term.

terms.definition: a certain or probable future sacrifice of economic benefits arising from present obligations of a particular entity to transfer assets or to provide services to other entities in the future as a result of a past transactions(s) or event(s). three essential characteristics: a) It embodies a present duty or responsibility to one or more other entities that entails settlement by probable future transfer or use of assets at a specified or determinable date, on occurrence of a specified event, or on demand; b) The duty or responsibility obligates a particular entity, leaving it little or no discretion to avoid the future sacrifice; and c) The transaction or other event obligating the entity has already happened.
examples: Unpaid claims are a liability, since the insurer already owes the money and cannot avoid paying it.

terms.definition: Coverage for legal liability from injuries or property damage caused by auto accidents.
examples: Auto liability covered the other driver's injuries and the damage to her vehicle after our insured ran the light.

terms.definition: Coverage that pays for damage or injuries you cause to others in an accident.
examples: Liability coverage pays the people you harm, not your own repairs.

terms.definition: Insurance against loss due to claims for damages because of bodily injury to other parties, which may include loss under a contractual liability agreement.
examples: Liability insurance paid the claim when a delivery driver knocked over a customer's display case.

terms.definition: Written statements harming reputation.
examples: The online review alleging fraud went beyond opinion and was sued as libel.

terms.definition: Claim on property as security for debt.
examples: The contractor registered a lien on the property when his invoice went unpaid.

terms.definition: insurance that pays the same benefit amount should the insured die during the term of the contract, or if the insured survives to the end of the specified coverage term or age.
examples: The life endowment paid the same amount whether he died during the term or lived to its final day.

terms.definition: a group life insurance that provides a face amount that is adjustable to the certificate holder and allows the certificate holder to vary the modal premium that is paid or to skip a payment so long as the certificate value is sufficient to keep the certificate in force, and under which separately identified interest credits (other than in connection with dividend accumulation, premium deposit funds or other supplementary accounts) and mortality and expense charges are made to individual certificates while providing minimum guaranteed values.
examples: The flexible premium adjustable certificate let the member skip a payment one month, drawing on the account value instead.

terms.definition: Policy paying a specified sum to beneficiaries upon the insured's death.
examples: Life insurance paid her children $400,000 after her death, tax-free and outside the estate.

terms.definition: a contract or agreement in which a policyholder agrees to sell or transfer ownership in all or part of a life insurance policy to a third party for compensation that is less than the expected death benefit of a policy.
examples: Through a life settlement the policyholder sold his policy to an investor for less than the death benefit but more than the surrender value.

terms.definition: a provision in some disability income policies to recoup lost wages for the term of disability or remainder of insured's life in case of permanent disability.
examples: The lifetime disability benefit continued the monthly payments for as long as the permanent disability lasted.

terms.definition: A temporary change in job assignment to accommodate work restrictions while an injured employee is healing.
examples: Light duty put the injured technician on parts inventory for six weeks while his shoulder healed.

terms.definition: Replacement with similar used property.
examples: The insurer replaced the damaged cabinets with like kind and quality, not with brand new custom units.

terms.definition: Maximum amount payable under a policy.
examples: The limit of liability on the policy is $1 million, so the insurer pays no more than that per occurrence.

terms.definition: Time allowed to bring legal action.
examples: The limitation period expired, so the injured party could no longer bring suit.

terms.definition: policies that provide coverage for vision, prescription drug, and/or any other single service plan or program. Also include short-term care policies that provide coverage for less than one year for medical and other services provided in a setting other than an acute care unit of the hospital.
examples: The vision and prescription drug plans are limited benefit policies, covering a single service rather than full medical care.

terms.definition: a form of whole-life insurance with a pre-defined number of premiums to be paid.
examples: He chose limited payment life insurance, paying premiums only until age sixty-five while coverage continues for life.

terms.definition: health insurance coverage for a certain ailment, such as cancer.
examples: The limited policy paid a lump sum on a cancer diagnosis but covered nothing else.

terms.definition: The maximum amount for which an insurer or pool may be liable for any loss during a specific period.
examples: The policy limits cap the insurer's exposure at $2 million however many claims arrive that year.

terms.definition: classification of business written by insurers.
examples: Auto, homeowners, and workers' compensation are each a separate line of business in the insurer's filings.

terms.definition: coverage for the liability of an entity involved in the retail or wholesale sales of alcoholic beverages, or the serving of alcoholic beverages, to persons who have incurred bodily injury or property damage arising from an intoxicated person.
examples: Liquor liability covered the pub when a patron it had served caused injuries after leaving.

terms.definition: A claim in which the claimant is represented by an attorney, or, in workers' compensation, one in which an application for adjudication has been filed.
examples: Once the claimant hired counsel, the file was reclassified as a litigated claim.

terms.definition: a rider attached to a life insurance policy providing long term care for the terminally ill.
examples: The living benefits rider let him draw on the death benefit early to pay for care during his terminal illness.

terms.definition: A corporation that maintains facilities for the insurance business of its underwriting and broker members, regulates membership, and disseminates information.
examples: The risk was placed at Lloyd's of London, which provides the marketplace rather than writing the policy itself.

terms.definition: A group of underwriters at Lloyd's, London who underwrite insurance as a group, with liability several among members in agreed proportions.
examples: The Lloyd's syndicate took a share of the satellite risk, with each member liable for its own agreed proportion.

terms.definition: A member of Lloyd's, London who underwrites insurance there.
examples: The Lloyd's underwriter reviewed the slip and initialled for a ten percent share.

terms.definition: Amount that can be borrowed using the policy as collateral.
examples: After fifteen years the policy's loan value let her borrow $18,000 against it without surrendering the coverage.

terms.definition: pass-through certificates, collateralized mortgage obligations (CMOs), and other securitized loans not included in structured securities where payment of interest and/or principal is directly proportional to the interest and/or principal received by the issuer from the mortgage pool or other underlying securities.
examples: Loan-backed securities pass through the mortgage pool's interest and principal directly to the investors.

terms.definition: contracts, excluding financial guaranty contracts, mortgage guaranty contracts and surety contracts, that fulfill both of the following conditions: (1) the contract term is greater than or equal to thirteen months and (2) the insurer can neither cancel nor increase the premium during the contract term.
examples: The eighteen-month policy is a long duration contract, since the insurer cannot cancel it or raise the premium midterm.

terms.definition: policies that provide coverage for not less than one year for diagnostic, preventive, therapeutic, rehabilitative, maintenance, or personal care services provided in a setting other than an acute care unit of a hospital, including policies that provide benefits for cognitive impairment or loss of functional capacity. This includes policies providing only nursing home care, home health care, community based care, or any combination. The policy does not include coverage provided under comprehensive/major medical policies, Medicare Advantage, or for accelerated death benefit-type products.
examples: Her long term care policy paid for home health aides and later for the nursing home.

terms.definition: policy providing monthly income payments for insureds who become disabled for an extensive length of time, typically two years or longer.
examples: Long term disability income insurance kept paying monthly benefits through the third year of his illness.

terms.definition: A benefit providing employees with partial income replacement if they become sick or injured and cannot work.
examples: LTD replaced sixty percent of his salary once the short-term benefits ran out.

terms.definition: Injury or damage sustained by an insured, or the amount for which an insurer or pool becomes liable upon occurrence of an insured event.
examples: The loss was the smoke-damaged inventory, and the insurer became liable for it the moment the fire started.

terms.definition: expected payments for costs to be incurred in connection with the adjustment and recording of losses. Can be classified into two broad categories: Defense and Cost Containment (DCC) and Adjusting and Other (AO). Can also be separated into (Allocated Loss Adjustment Expense) and (Unallocated Loss Adjustment Expense for ratemaking purposes.
examples: Loss adjustment expense covers the money spent investigating and defending claims, not the claim payments themselves.

terms.definition: Methods of reducing the frequency and severity of losses, including avoidance, prevention, reduction, segregation of exposure units, and non-insurance risk transfer.
examples: Loss control put guards on the presses and moved the solvent store off site, cutting both claim frequency and severity.

terms.definition: The phenomenon of change in reported or paid losses for a particular accident year at different points in time.
examples: Loss development showed the 2023 accident year growing by twelve percent between its first and second evaluations.

terms.definition: A factor applied to losses from an accident year evaluated at one point in time to project the losses for the same year at a later evaluation point.
examples: A loss development factor of 1.15 projects that reported losses will grow another fifteen percent before they settle.

terms.definition: incidence of claims on a policy during a premium period.
examples: The fleet's loss frequency rose to eleven claims per hundred vehicles this year.

terms.definition: policy providing protection against loss of use due to damage or destruction of property.
examples: Loss of use insurance paid the rental income the landlord could not collect while the unit was uninhabitable.

terms.definition: coverage for third party mortgagee in case of default on insured property, secured by a loan, that has been lost or damaged.
examples: The loss payable clause directed part of the fire settlement to the bank holding the mortgage.

terms.definition: the percentage of incurred losses to earned premiums.
examples: A loss ratio of 68 means sixty-eight cents of every earned premium dollar went to claims.

terms.definition: the amount that insurers set aside to cover claims incurred but not yet paid.
examples: The insurer's loss reserve holds the money set aside for claims already incurred but not yet paid.

terms.definition: an estimate of liability or provision in an insurer's financial statement, indicating the amount the insurer expects to pay for losses incurred but not yet reported or reported claims that haven't been paid.
examples: Loss reserves on the balance sheet estimate both reported claims awaiting payment and those not yet reported.

terms.definition: Includes claims that have been paid and/or have amounts held in reserve for future payment
examples: Losses incurred include the cheques already written plus the reserves held for what is still to come.

terms.definition: Covers damage to a company's machinery or equipment due to fire, theft, accident, or technical failure.
examples: Machinery insurance paid to repair the press after a bearing failure wrecked the drive assembly.

terms.definition: a hospital/surgical/medical expense contract that provides comprehensive benefits as defined in the state in which the contract will be delivered.
examples: The major medical contract covers hospital stays, surgery, and physician care up to the state-defined benefit levels.

terms.definition: Alleged professional misconduct or lack of ordinary skill in the performance of a professional act.
examples: The suit alleged malpractice, claiming the surgeon had fallen short of the ordinary standard of care.

terms.definition: Coverage for professional negligence.
examples: Malpractice insurance covered the physician's defence costs and the eventual settlement.

terms.definition: system of health care delivery that attempts to influence the utilization, quality, and cost of services provided.
examples: Managed care required a referral before the specialist visit, steering both the cost and the choice of provider.

terms.definition: Business authorized to solicit insurance for companies.
examples: The managing general agent underwrote and issued policies on the insurer's behalf within agreed limits.

terms.definition: insurance required by state or federal law.
examples: State law made maternity coverage a mandated benefit, so the plan could not exclude it.

terms.definition: A required conference to discuss settlement of disputed issues prior to trial.
examples: At the mandatory settlement conference the parties narrowed the disputed issues before trial.

terms.definition: provides broad form coverage of personal property of an insured manufacturer including raw material, goods in process, finished goods and goods shipped to customers.
examples: The manufacturers output policy covered raw steel, goods on the line, finished stock, and shipments to customers.

terms.definition: The theoretical probability of a particular outcome assuming a value less than a specified confidence level.
examples: The actuary built in a margin for adverse experience so the reserve would hold up in a bad year.

terms.definition: a deposit that an organization is required to maintain with a broker with respect to the Futures Contracts purchased or sold.
examples: The insurer posted margin premium with its broker to maintain the futures positions in its hedging program.

terms.definition: Coverage for goods in transit and transportation vehicles on waterways, land, and air.
examples: Marine insurance covered the containers of coffee from the port of loading to the warehouse door.

terms.definition: fair value or the price that could be derived from current sale of an asset.
examples: The building's market value is what a willing buyer would pay today, which may differ from its insured value.

terms.definition: False statement of important fact on an application, such as garage location.
examples: Saying the car was garaged in a small town while it actually sat downtown was a material misrepresentation.

terms.definition: premiums attributable to policies covering repair or replacement service, or indemnification for that service, for the operational or structural failure of property due to defects in materials or workmanship, or normal wear and tear. (May cover motor vehicles, mobile equipment, boats, appliances, electronics, residual structures, etc.)
examples: Mechanical breakdown insurance paid for the transmission failure that the manufacturer's warranty no longer covered.

terms.definition: policies issued in association with the Federal/State entitlement program created by Title XIX of the Social Security Act of 1965 that pays for medical assistance for certain individuals and families with low incomes and resources.
examples: Medicaid covered the family's medical costs because their income fell below the program's threshold.

terms.term: Medical and Hospital Expenses (Benefits or Claims)
terms.definition: total expenditures for health care services paid to or on behalf of members.
examples: The plan's medical and hospital expenses totalled what it paid providers on behalf of its members that year.

terms.definition: A form releasing the medical information of an involved party.
examples: The adjuster could not obtain the hospital records until the claimant signed a medical authorization form.

terms.definition: The complete medical record of a patient at a medical facility.
examples: The nurse case manager reviewed the medical file to see whether the treatment matched the reported injury.

terms.definition: insurance coverage protecting a licensed health care provider or health care facility against legal liability resulting from the death or injury of any person due to the insured's misconduct, negligence, or incompetence, in rendering or failure to render professional services.
examples: Medical malpractice coverage responded when a patient sued the clinic over a delayed diagnosis.

terms.definition: A bodily injury or professional negligence claim arising from the provision or administration of medical treatment.
examples: The suit over the surgical error was handled as a medical malpractice claim.

terms.definition: line of business that provides medical only benefits without hospital coverage. An example would be provider-sponsored organizations where there is no coverage for other than provider (non-hospital) services. Does not include self-insured business, FEHBP, Medicare and Medicaid programs, or dental only business.
examples: The medical only line covers physician and clinic services with no hospital benefits attached.

terms.definition: A work-related injury claim in which there is no lost time away from work.
examples: The stitched hand was a medical only claim, since the worker finished his shift and lost no time.

terms.definition: Pays reasonable medical or funeral expenses due to bodily injury from an auto accident.
examples: Medical payments covered the passenger's ambulance and emergency room bills without waiting for a fault decision.

terms.definition: Coverage paying medical expenses for you and passengers injured in an accident.
examples: Medical payments coverage paid for her own treatment and her passengers' after the crash.

terms.definition: insurance coverage protecting a licensed health care provider or health care facility against legal liability resulting from the death or injury of any person due to the insured's misconduct, negligence, or incompetence in rendering professional services. Medical Professional Liability is also known as Medical Malpractice.
examples: Medical professional liability protects the physician against claims that her care fell below the professional standard.

terms.definition: Under California workers' compensation, an entity or group of providers approved by the state's workers' compensation administrative director.
examples: Under the medical provider network the injured worker chose a treating doctor from the approved list.

terms.definition: Treatment reasonably required to cure or relieve a claimant or employee from the effects of a liability claim or work-related injury or illness, including prescriptions and prescribed durable medical equipment.
examples: Medical treatment included the surgery, the physiotherapy, and the back brace prescribed afterwards.

terms.definition: A person who has enrolled as a subscriber or an eligible dependent of a subscriber and for whom the health organization has accepted the responsibility for the provision of health services as may be contracted for.
examples: Each member of the plan, whether employee or dependent, is entitled to the contracted health services.

terms.definition: The lowest premium or contribution for which an insurer or pool will cover a risk for a specified period.
examples: The insurer's minimum premium of $500 applies even when the exposure would calculate to less.

terms.definition: an arrangement under which an insurance carrier will, for a fee, handle the administration of claims and insure against large claims for a self-insured group. The employer self-funds a fixed percentage (e.g. 90%) of the estimated monthly claims, and the insurer covers the remainder.
examples: Under the minimum premium plan the employer funds ninety percent of expected claims and the insurer covers the rest.

terms.definition: Includes coverage for lightning, windstorm, tornado, earthquake, and entertainment production interruption.
examples: Miscellaneous insurance picked up the lightning, windstorm, and production interruption exposures not written elsewhere.

terms.definition: An incorrect estimate of the insurance premium.
examples: The agent's misquote of $900 had to be corrected to $1,400 once the vehicle details were verified.

terms.definition: General liability coverage for land vehicles, self-propelled or not, that are not subject to motor vehicle registration.
examples: Mobile equipment coverage applied to the yard forklift, which never needed a licence plate.

terms.definition: Homeowners - homeowners insurance sold to owners occupying the described mobile home.
examples: The mobile homes policy insured the unit, its attached deck, and the owner's belongings inside.

terms.definition: coverage for mobile homes while under transport for personal or commercial use.
examples: Coverage for mobile homes under transport applied while the unit was being hauled to the new site.

terms.definition: an annuity that contains a provision that adjusts the value of withdrawn funds based on a formula in the contract. The formula reflects market value adjustments.
examples: The modified guaranteed annuity applied a market value adjustment when she withdrew funds early.

terms.definition: A modification of an injured employee's usual and customary job, designed to accommodate a qualified injured worker until release to full duty; also called transitional duty.
examples: A modified job kept the injured packer at work, sorting light items until he was released to full duty.

terms.definition: personality characteristics that increase probability of losses. For example not taking proper care to protect insured property because the insured knows the insurance company will replace it if it is damaged or stolen.
examples: Moral hazard shows up when an insured leaves the shop unlocked because he knows the stock is covered.

terms.definition: negligence or disregard on the part of the insured which could lead to probable loss.
examples: Morale hazard is the careless attitude that makes losses more likely, like ignoring the dripping sprinkler valve.

terms.definition: the frequency or severity of disease or illness within a subset of the population.
examples: Morbidity data showed how often the illness occurred among workers in that age group.

terms.definition: the potential for a person to experience illness, injury, or other physical or psychological impairment, whether temporary or permanent. Morbidity risk excludes the potential for an individual's death, but includes the potential for an illness or injury that results in death.
examples: Morbidity risk covers the chance of illness or injury, including one that later proves fatal, but not death itself.

terms.definition: a statistical record of the rate of illness among the defined age groups.
examples: The morbidity table showed illness rates rising sharply for insureds over sixty.

terms.definition: chart that shows the death rates of a particular population at each age displayed as the number of deaths per thousand.
examples: The mortality table gave the expected deaths per thousand at each age, which the actuary used to price the policy.

terms.definition: a note used to secure a loan for real property.
examples: The mortgage secures the loan against the house, giving the lender a claim if payments stop.

terms.definition: insurance that indemnifies a lender for loss upon foreclosure if a borrower fails to meet required mortgage payments.
examples: Mortgage guaranty insurance repaid the lender part of its loss when the borrower defaulted and the sale fell short.

terms.definition: a form of life insurance coverage payable to a third party lender/mortgagee upon the death of the insured/mortgagor for loss of loan payments.
examples: Mortgage insurance paid the outstanding balance directly to the lender when the borrower died.

terms.definition: a type of asset-backed security that is secured by a mortgage or collection of mortgages. These securities must also be grouped in one of the top two ratings as determined by an accredited credit rating agency, and usually pay periodic payments that are similar to coupon payments. Furthermore, the mortgage must have originated from a regulated and authorized financial institution.
examples: The insurer's portfolio included mortgage-backed securities rated in the top two categories.

terms.definition: A clause making coverage proceeds payable to a named mortgagee, as its interest may appear, and stating the terms of the agreement between the insurer and the mortgagee.
examples: The mortgagee clause made the fire settlement payable to the bank as its interest appeared.

terms.definition: A state-issued record of your driving history used by insurers to assess risk.
examples: The underwriter pulled a motor vehicle report and found an at-fault accident from last spring.

terms.definition: Movable property such as furniture, machinery, and other equipment that can be insured.
examples: The policy covered movables such as the office furniture, the workshop machinery, and the display cabinets.

terms.definition: personal and business property coverage combining several types of property insurance in one policy.
examples: The multi peril policy bundled fire, theft, and water damage coverage for the shop into one contract.

terms.definition: A discount for purchasing multiple insurance policies from the same company.
examples: Insuring both the house and the cars with one company earned her a multi-policy discount.

terms.definition: coverage sold to municipalities to guarantee the principle payment on bonds issued.
examples: Municipal bond guarantee insurance assured investors that the principal on the town's bonds would be repaid.

terms.definition: liability coverage for the acts of a municipality.
examples: Municipal liability covered the city when a cyclist was hurt on a poorly maintained bike path.

terms.definition: any security, or other instrument, including a state lease but not a lease of any other governmental entity, under which a payment obligation is created, issued by or on behalf of a governmental unit to finance a project servicing a substantial public purpose, and 1) Payable from tax revenues, but not tax allocations, within the jurisdiction of such governmental unit; 2) Payable or guaranteed by the United States of America or any agency, department or instrumentality thereof, or by a state housing agency; 3) Payable from rates or charges (but not tolls) levied or collected in respect of a non-nuclear utility project, public transportation facility (other than an airport facility) or public higher education facility; or 4) With respect to lease obligations, payable from future appropriations.
examples: The municipal obligation bond funded a water treatment plant and is repaid from the charges levied on users.

terms.definition: a privately held insurer owned by its policyholders, operated as a non-profit that may or may not be incorporated.
examples: As a mutual insurance company it is owned by its policyholders, so surplus returns to them rather than to shareholders.

terms.definition: a company organized as a mutual and owning a capital stock insurer or insurers for the benefit of pooling risk for many people, typically those in the same industry.
examples: The mutual insurance holding company owns the stock insurer while remaining member-owned itself.

terms.definition: The entity with whom an insurance contract is made and who is specifically designated by name as protected.
examples: The named insured is the person listed on the declarations, with the fullest rights under the policy.

terms.definition: insurance for losses explicitly defined in the policy contract.
examples: Named peril coverage listed fire, lightning, and theft, so the water damage claim was denied.

terms.definition: A policy type that specifies the particular perils covered.
examples: Under a named perils form only the listed causes are covered, and anything not listed is not.

terms.definition: Fidelity bond covering persons listed on the bond.
examples: The named schedule bond covered the three employees listed by name who handled cash.

terms.definition: A national organization of state officials charged with the regulation of insurance.
examples: The NAIC develops model laws that individual states then adapt into their own insurance regulation.

terms.definition: A statistical and rate-making organization for insurers and pools offering workers' compensation coverage.
examples: NCCI collects the payroll and claims data used to set workers' compensation rates in most states.

terms.definition: refers to rating organizations so designated by the SEC whose status has been confirmed by the Securities Valuation Office. Examples are: Moody's Investors Service, Inc., Standard and Poor's (SandP), A.M. Best Company (A.M. Best) and Fitch Ratings and Dominion Bond Rating Service (DBRS).
examples: The bond's rating came from an NRSRO, one of the agencies whose ratings the regulator accepts.

terms.definition: A hazard existing naturally in the environment, not artificially created.
examples: Living on a floodplain is a natural hazard, present in the environment rather than created by the owner.

terms.definition: The diagnosis and type of injury or damage (nature) and the degree of its severity (extent).
examples: The report described the nature and extent of the injury: a fractured tibia, healing without permanent restriction.
lookup_keys: nature extent of injury or damages

terms.definition: A tort consisting of a failure to do something, or the doing of something, that a reasonable person would not do under the circumstances.
examples: Leaving a spill unmarked for an hour was negligence, since a reasonable manager would have coned it off.

terms.definition: The unexcused violation of a statute, constituting automatic or self-evident negligence.
examples: Running the red light was negligence per se, because the statute itself was violated with no excuse offered.

terms.definition: total of assets whose values are permitted by state law to be included in the annual statement of the insurer.
examples: Net admitted assets exclude the furniture and overdue receivables that state law will not let the insurer count.

terms.definition: total revenues from an insurer's operations less total expenses and income taxes
examples: Net income for the year was what remained after claims, expenses, and taxes were taken from total revenue.

terms.definition: premiums on property/casualty or health policies that will not have to be returned to the policyholder if the policy is cancelled.
examples: Net premiums earned represent the portion the insurer keeps even if the policy is cancelled tomorrow.

terms.definition: National Flood Insurance Program - flood insurance and floodplain management for personal and business property administered under the National Flood Act of 1968. Encourages participation by private insurers through a flood insurance pool .
examples: The NFIP wrote the flood policy, since private carriers would not cover the floodplain property.

terms.definition: Coverage that pays for losses regardless of who is at fault; often called PIP.
examples: Under no-fault insurance her own insurer paid her medical bills regardless of who caused the collision.

terms.definition: insurers in which a parent company has: 1) a financial interest represented by the direct or indirect ownership of less than 50% of voting shares, and 2) does not have the ability to exercise control over the insurer, e.g., through voting stock or management contract
examples: The parent owns thirty percent of the carrier and cannot direct its decisions, so it is a non-controlled stock insurer.

terms.definition: reinsurance that is not secured on individual lives for specific individual amount of reinsurance, but rather reinsurance that protects the ceding company's overall experience on its entire portfolio of business, or at least a broad segment of it. The most common forms of non-proportional reinsurance are stop loss and catastrophe.
examples: Non-proportional reinsurance protects the whole portfolio once total losses cross a threshold, rather than sharing each policy.

terms.definition: assets having economic value other than those which can be used to fulfill policyholder obligations, or those assets which are unavailable due to encumbrances or other third party interests and should not be recognized on the balance sheet.
examples: Furniture and overdue agents' balances are nonadmitted assets and are kept off the statutory balance sheet.

terms.definition: An insurer not licensed to do business in the jurisdiction in question.
examples: The nonadmitted insurer wrote the risk through surplus lines because it holds no licence in that state.

terms.definition: The transfer of a loss exposure to another party, such as through indemnity or hold-harmless agreements, or by being named an additional insured under another's policy.
examples: Requiring the subcontractor to sign a hold-harmless is a noninsurance transfer of the exposure.

terms.definition: the principal value upon which future payments are based in a derivative transaction as at a specific period in time (the "as of" reporting date) in the reporting currency.
examples: The swap's notional value of $50 million is the reference amount, not money that changes hands.

terms.definition: coverage for bodily injury and property damage liability resulting from the nuclear energy material (whether or not radioactive) on the insured business's premises or in transit.
examples: Nuclear energy liability covered bodily injury claims arising from radioactive material at the facility and in transit.

terms.definition: A registered nurse assigned by a self-insured entity, insurer, or third-party administrator to monitor medical treatment.
examples: The nurse case manager attended appointments and kept the treatment plan and return-to-work goals aligned.

terms.definition: The person or organization protected by a bond.
examples: The obligee on the performance bond is the project owner, who is protected if the contractor fails.

terms.definition: Principal bound by an obligation; both principal and surety are obligors.
examples: Both the contractor and its surety are obligors, each bound to perform under the bond.

terms.definition: An accident occurring in the course of employment and caused by an occupational hazard.
examples: The chemical burn was an occupational accident, caused by a hazard specific to the plating line.

terms.definition: A health impairment arising out of and in the course of employment, caused by conditions peculiar to a particular trade or occupation.
examples: Years of solvent exposure caused an occupational disease peculiar to that trade rather than a single accident.

terms.definition: an accident , including injurious exposure to conditions, which results, during the policy period in bodily injury or property damage neither expected or intended from the standpoint of the insured. (Bickelhaupt and Magee)
examples: The slow leak counted as one occurrence, since the damage came from continuous exposure the insured never intended.

terms.definition: coverage for ocean and inland water transportation exposures; goods or cargoes; ships or hulls; earnings; and liability.
examples: Ocean marine covered the hull, the cargo, the freight earnings, and the shipowner's liability.

terms.definition: a president, vice-president, treasurer, actuary, secretary, controller and any other person who performs for the company functions corresponding to those performed by the foregoing officers.
examples: Each officer, from the president to the controller, must be listed in the company's annual filing.

terms.definition: an agreement giving the buyer the right to buy or receive, sell or deliver, enter into, extend or terminate, or effect a cash settlement based on the actual or expected price, level, performance or value of one or more Underlying Interests.
examples: The option gave the insurer the right, but not the obligation, to sell the bonds at a set price.

terms.definition: Additional coverage you can add to your insurance to extend what's covered.
examples: She added optional coverage for rental car reimbursement and roadside assistance.

terms.definition: Under workers' compensation, an order that places a claim in an inactive status.
examples: The order taking off calendar moved the claim to inactive status until either party asked for a hearing.

terms.definition: accident and health coverages not otherwise properly classified as Group Accident and Health or Credit Accident and Health (e.g., collectively renewable and individual non-cancelable, guaranteed renewable, non-renewable for stated reasons only, etc.). Include all Medicare Part D Prescription Drug Coverage, whether sold on a stand-alone basis or through a Medicare Advantage product and whether sold directly to an individual or through a group.
examples: Guaranteed renewable individual policies and Medicare Part D drug plans are reported under other accident and health.

terms.definition: Unallocated annuity considerations and other unallocated deposits that incorporate any mortality or morbidity risk and are not reported as direct premiums, direct annuity considerations or deposit-type contract funds.
examples: Unallocated annuity deposits carrying mortality risk are reported as other considerations rather than as premium.

terms.definition: A clause stating the effect of other insurance on a coverage agreement.
examples: The other insurance clause made this policy pay only its share when a second policy covered the same loss.

terms.definition: coverage protecting the insured against legal liability resulting from negligence, carelessness, or a failure to act resulting in property damage or personal injury to others.
examples: Other liability covered the property damage claim arising from the insured's careless handling of a customer's equipment.

terms.definition: allocable expenses other than loss adjustment expenses and investment expenses.
examples: Other underwriting expenses include commissions, salaries, and taxes, but not claim handling or investment costs.

terms.definition: When you pay for more insurance than you actually need.
examples: Insuring a $200,000 house for $400,000 is over-insurance: the extra premium buys protection the owner can never collect.

terms.definition: homeowners insurance sold to owners occupying the described property.
examples: The owner occupied policy applies because the family lives in the house rather than renting it out.

terms.definition: Title insurance protecting the homeowner against claims on the property.
examples: The buyer's owner's policy protects her own title if an old lien surfaces years after closing.

terms.definition: two or more distinct policies combined into a single contract.
examples: The package policy combined property, general liability, and crime coverage into a single contract with one renewal date.

terms.definition: The total amount actually paid for a claim or group of claims, including loss adjustment expenses and legal fees.
examples: Paid losses on the file total $47,000, counting the settlement, the defence fees, and the medical bills.

terms.definition: Under California workers' compensation, one of a list of three independent qualified medical evaluators from which an unrepresented injured employee selects one for evaluation.
examples: Because he had no lawyer, the unrepresented worker picked one physician from the panel of three qualified medical evaluators.

terms.definition: the nominal or face value of a stock or bond.
examples: The bond has a par value of $1,000 even though it currently trades at $960.

terms.definition: A loss of less than the entire value of property.
examples: The kitchen fire was a partial loss, since most of the house remained sound.

terms.definition: The body part injured in an accident, used along with the nature of injury to assist in training and analysis.
examples: Coding the injured part of the body as the lower back helps the safety team target its training.

terms.definition: The insurer, insured, injured worker, claims administrator, employer, attorney, or any other person or group with an interest in a claim.
examples: Every party to the claim, from the employer to the treating physician, received notice of the hearing.

terms.definition: A clause providing for payment of a loss to a person or class of persons.
examples: The payee clause directed the settlement to the leasing company rather than to the driver.

terms.definition: A bond guaranteeing the construction of an improvement in connection with which a lender provides financing to the owner.
examples: The performance bond guaranteed the school would be built even if the contractor walked off the job.

terms.definition: the cause of property damage or personal injury, origin of desire for insurance. "Cause of Loss"
examples: Fire, hail, and theft are perils, the causes of loss the policy either covers or excludes.

terms.definition: A description of an injured employee's condition when it will neither improve nor deteriorate, as determined by the treating physician and a prerequisite to determining permanent disability.
examples: The doctor declared the condition permanent and stationary, which allowed the permanent disability rating to be calculated.

terms.definition: Payments to a worker whose job injury permanently limits the type and scope of work the employee can perform.
examples: Permanent disability payments began once it was clear he could never return to overhead welding.

terms.definition: A voluntary lump-sum payment on the undisputed portion of permanent disability due in the future.
examples: The insurer made a permanent disability advance on the undisputed portion while the rest was still being argued.

terms.definition: The determination of the level of permanent disability based on a physician's medical report, expressed as a numeric percentage from 1% to 100%.
examples: The permanent disability rating came back at 34 percent based on the physician's report.

terms.definition: policy that remains active for the life of the insured.
examples: Permanent life insurance stays in force for the insured's whole life, unlike a twenty-year term policy.

terms.definition: Benefits paid to a worker capable of working but whose ability to compete in the open labor market is reduced.
examples: Permanent partial disability benefits recognised that he could still work but had lost some earning ability.

terms.definition: Payments to a worker considered permanently unable to compete in the open labor market due to a complete and permanent loss of earning power.
examples: Permanent total disability payments continue for life, since the worker can no longer compete for any job.

terms.definition: coverage designed to insure private passenger automobiles and certain types of trucks owned by an individual or husband and wife.
examples: The personal auto policy covered the couple's sedan and their light pickup for family use.

terms.definition: earthquake property coverage for personal, family or household purposes.
examples: Personal earthquake coverage paid to repair the family home's cracked foundation after the tremor.

terms.definition: separate flood insurance policy sold for personal, family or household purposes.
examples: Because the house sits near the river, the owner bought a separate personal flood policy.

terms.definition: credit insurance that insures the excess of the outstanding indebtedness over the primary property insurance benefits in the event of a total loss to a collateral asset.
examples: Personal GAP insurance paid the $4,200 still owed on the loan after the insurer settled the totalled car at market value.

terms.definition: An injury to a person.
examples: The claim covered personal injury to the passenger, who suffered a broken collarbone.

terms.definition: Liability insurance covering libel, slander, false arrest, and similar offenses.
examples: Personal injury insurance covered the newspaper when a subject of an article sued for libel.

terms.definition: liability coverage for those who have been discriminated against, falsely arrested, illegally detained, libeled, maliciously prosecuted, slandered, suffered from identity theft, mental anguish or alienation of affections, or have had their right of privacy violated.
examples: Personal injury liability covered the store after a customer was wrongly detained by a security guard.

terms.definition: automobile coverage available in states that have enacted no-fault laws or other auto reparation reform laws for treatment of injuries to the insured and passengers of the insured.
examples: PIP paid for the driver's and passengers' treatment without waiting for the fault investigation to finish.

terms.definition: single interest or dual interest credit insurance (where collateral is not a motor vehicle, mobile home, or real estate) that covers perils to goods purchased or used as collateral and that concerns a creditor's interest in the purchased goods or pledged collateral either in whole or in part; or covers perils to goods purchased in connection with an open-end credit transaction.
examples: The lender arranged personal property coverage on the financed appliances used as collateral.

terms.definition: veterinary care plan insurance policy providing care for a pet animal (e.g., dog or cat) of the insured owner in the event of its illness or accident.
examples: The pet insurance plan covered the dog's surgery after he swallowed a toy.

terms.definition: An appeal of a decision issued by a workers' compensation administrative law judge, typically filed within 20-30 days of the final decision.
examples: The worker filed a petition for reconsideration within twenty days of the judge's final decision.

terms.definition: Tangible evidence that verifies a loss, such as photographs, statements, or contractual documents.
examples: Photographs of the damaged pallets and the signed delivery receipt were the physical evidence supporting the claim.

terms.definition: A detailed schedule of activities aimed at the efficient resolution of a claim, project, or assignment.
examples: The adjuster's plan of action set out the site visit, the recorded statement, and the reserve review with dates for each.

terms.definition: A contract between an insurer and insured outlining coverage, exclusions, and conditions.
examples: The policy runs to forty pages, covering what is insured, what is excluded, and what the insured must do.

terms.definition: a refund of part of the premium on a participating life insurance policy. Amount of payment is determined by subtracting the actual premium expense from the premium charged. The payment can be taken as cash, applied to a purchase an increment of paid-up insurance, left on deposit with the insurance company or applied to purchase term insurance for one year.
examples: Her participating policy paid a policy dividend, which she used to buy a small amount of paid-up insurance.

terms.definition: A document containing all general and specific insurance terms.
examples: The policy document sets out the general conditions along with the specific terms for her coverage.

terms.definition: Maximum amount a policy will pay under a coverage.
examples: The policy limit of $300,000 capped what the insurer paid, leaving the rest to the insured.

terms.definition: time period during which insurance coverage is in effect.
examples: The policy period runs from June 1 this year to June 1 next, and only losses inside it are covered.

terms.definition: the amount of money allocated specifically for the fulfillment of policy obligations by a life insurance company; reserves are in place to safeguard that the company is able to pay all future claims.
examples: The life insurer holds a policy reserve so that future death claims can be paid when they arise.

terms.definition: A coverage and claim experience period that includes the claims covered by a policy written in that year, regardless of whether the claims have yet been reported.
examples: Policy year results group all claims arising from policies written that year, whenever those claims eventually surface.

terms.definition: The person who has entered into the agreement with the insurer.
examples: The policyholder pays the premium and decides whether to renew, cancel, or change the coverage.

terms.definition: assets in excess of the liabilities of a company or net income above any monies indebted to legal obligation.
examples: Policyholders surplus is the cushion left when the insurer's liabilities are subtracted from its assets.

terms.definition: environmental contamination.
examples: The claim involved pollution: solvent had seeped from a cracked tank into the soil.

terms.definition: an association organized for the purpose of absorbing losses through a risk-sharing mechanism thereby limiting individual exposures.
examples: Twelve school boards formed a pool so that no single district would bear a catastrophic claim alone.

terms.definition: Authority given to a person or corporation, called an attorney-in-fact, to act for and obligate another to a specified extent.
examples: The power of attorney let the attorney-in-fact sign the settlement documents on the claimant's behalf.

terms.definition: Under California workers' compensation, a personal physician an employee designates in writing, before an injury occurs, to provide treatment if a job injury happens.
examples: Because she had named a pre-designated physician in writing before her injury, her own doctor treated her.

terms.definition: Damage or injury that existed prior to the occurrence or incident claimed.
examples: The MRI showed a pre-existing injury: the disc had degenerated well before the reported fall.

terms.definition: Under workers' compensation, the work performed on the date of injury, including all its duties, demands, obligations, and terms.
examples: Returning to pre-injury work means resuming every duty and demand of the job he held the day he was hurt.

terms.definition: arrangement, insured or uninsured, where contracts are established by Health Plan Companies (typically, commercial insurers, and, in some circumstances, by self-insured employers) with health care providers. The Health Plans involved will often designate these contracted providers as "preferred" and will provide an incentive, usually in the form of lower deductibles or co-payments, to encourage covered individuals to use these providers. Members are allowed benefits for non-participating provider services on an indemnity basis with significant copayments and providers are often, but not always, paid on a discounted fee for service basis.
examples: Using a PPO doctor cost her a $25 copay, while going outside the network doubled her share of the bill.

terms.definition: insured, or applicant for insurance, who presents likelihood of risk lower than that of the standard applicant.
examples: A non-smoking driver with a clean record and a garaged car is a preferred risk and gets the lowest rate.

terms.definition: The particular location, or portion of it, defined by a coverage agreement.
examples: The policy defines the premises as the leased suite on the third floor, not the whole building.

terms.definition: policies covering the liability of an insured to persons who have incurred bodily injury or property damage on an insured's premises during normal operations or routine maintenance, or from an insured's business operations either on or off of the insured's premises.
examples: Premises and operations covered the customer's fall in the showroom and the damage the crew caused at a client's site.

terms.definition: The total annual cost of insurance or membership fees charged to an insured or pool member.
examples: The annual premium came to $2,400, payable monthly.

terms.definition: A plan providing percentage reductions in premiums or contributions that increase with the size of the risk.
examples: The premium discount plan reduced the rate as the payroll grew, since larger accounts cost proportionally less to service.

terms.definition: A lender pays the premium; the policyholder repays with interest.
examples: Rather than pay $60,000 up front, the company used premium financing and repaid the lender monthly with interest.

terms.definition: The price per unit of coverage.
examples: The premium rate is $1.20 per $100 of payroll, so the total depends on the size of the crew.

terms.definition: the portion of premium for which the policy protection or coverage has already been given during the now-expired portion of the policy term.
examples: Six months into an annual policy, half the premium has become premiums earned.

terms.definition: is the amount calculated on the basis of the interest and mortality table used to calculate the reporting entity's statutory policy reserves.
examples: Premiums net are calculated from the interest and mortality assumptions used for the statutory reserves.

terms.definition: total premiums generated from all policies (contracts) written by an insurer within a given period of time.
examples: Premiums written total everything the insurer sold this quarter, whether or not the coverage has been provided yet.

terms.definition: coverage that takes precedence when more than one policy covers the same loss.
examples: The homeowner's policy was primary, and the umbrella paid only after its limits were exhausted.

terms.definition: Under workers' compensation, the physician with overall responsibility for treating an employee's industrial injury or illness; only one PTP may exist at a time.
examples: The primary treating physician writes the reports and coordinates all care, and only one may hold that role at a time.

terms.definition: The person or organization whose obligations are guaranteed by a surety.
examples: The contractor is the principal on the bond, and the surety guarantees his performance to the owner.

terms.definition: a state regulatory requirement for pre-approval of all insurance rates and forms.
examples: Under the state's prior approval law the insurer had to wait for the regulator to sign off before using the new rates.

terms.definition: filings that include singularly or in any combination coverage such as the following: Auto Liability, Personal Injury Protection (PIP), Medical Payments (MP), Uninsured/Underinsured (UM/UIM); Specified Causes of Loss, Comprehensive, and Collision.
examples: The private passenger auto filing bundled liability, medical payments, comprehensive, and collision coverages.

terms.definition: An injured worker or other claimant not represented by an attorney.
examples: Appearing pro per, the worker presented his own case without an attorney.

terms.definition: portion of the losses and premium reinsurer shares with the ceding entity.
examples: Under pro rata reinsurance the reinsurer takes thirty percent of the premium and pays thirty percent of every loss.

terms.definition: A premium rate charged for a short term at the same proportion of the full-term rate as the short term bears to the full term.
examples: The pro-rata cancellation refunded four months of an annual premium when the policy was cancelled early.

terms.definition: an individual who sells, services, or negotiates insurance policies either on behalf of a company or independently.
examples: The producer earned commission on each policy she wrote and serviced.

terms.definition: insurance coverage protecting the manufacturer, distributor, seller, or lessor of a product against legal liability resulting from a defective condition causing personal injury, or damage, to any individual or entity, associated with the use of the product.
examples: Product liability covered the manufacturer when a defective heater element started a customer's kitchen fire.

terms.definition: Coverage against claims for damages arising from the handling, use of, or any condition in, products manufactured, sold, handled, or distributed by the insured.
examples: Products liability insurance responded to claims from consumers injured by a contaminated batch of supplements.

terms.definition: coverage available to pay for liability arising out of the performance of professional or business related duties, with coverage being tailored to the needs of the specific profession. Examples include abstracters, accountants, insurance adjusters, architects, engineers, insurance agents and brokers, lawyers, real estate agents, stockbrokers.
examples: Professional errors and omissions liability covered the architect after a design flaw forced expensive rework.

terms.definition: A claim arising from professional negligence, such as errors and omissions.
examples: The engineer's missed load calculation became a professional liability claim.

terms.definition: A physician's opinion of the future course of an injury or illness.
examples: The doctor's prognosis was full recovery within four months with physiotherapy.

terms.definition: A formal written statement of a claim for payment of loss, with supporting data.
examples: The insurer asked for a proof of loss listing the stolen items, their values, and the purchase receipts.

terms.definition: coverage protecting the insured against loss or damage to real or personal property from a variety of perils, including but not limited to fire, lightening, business interruption, loss of rents, glass breakage, tornado, windstorm, hail, water damage, explosion, riot, civil commotion, rain, or damage from aircraft or vehicles.
examples: Property coverage paid for the fire damage, the broken windows, and the rent lost while repairs were done.

terms.definition: Damage to another person's property covered under liability insurance.
examples: Property damage liability paid to repair the fence and mailbox his truck destroyed.

terms.definition: Coverage against claims for damages because of injury to others' property.
examples: Property damage liability insurance covered the claim when the crane dropped a beam on a neighbouring roof.

terms.definition: A small property loss allegation or claim, typically under a modest dollar threshold.
examples: The dented mailbox was logged as a small property loss allegation, below the threshold for a full investigation.

terms.definition: an insurance-linked security retained within the insurance or reinsurance company and is used to insulate the proceeds of the securities offering from the general business risks of the insurer, granting an additional comfort level for investors of the securitized instrument.
examples: The protected cell kept the securitized funds separate from the insurer's other business, reassuring investors.

terms.definition: a broad form of marine legal liability insurance coverage.
examples: Protection and indemnity insurance covered the shipowner's liability for crew injury and dock damage.

terms.definition: formal affiliations of providers, sometimes called "integrated delivery systems", organized and operated to provide an integrated network of health care providers with which third parties, such as insurance companies, HMOs, or other Health Plan Companies, may contract for health care services to covered individuals. Some models of integration include Physician Hospital Organizations, Management Service Organizations, Group Practices Without Walls, Medical Foundations, and Health Provider Cooperatives.
examples: The hospital and its affiliated physician groups formed a provider sponsored network that insurers could contract with.

terms.definition: contingencies outlined in an insurance policy.
examples: The policy provisions spell out what happens if the insured moves, cancels, or reports a claim late.

terms.definition: A cause of loss that results in an event in continuous sequence, without any other effective intervening cause.
examples: The storm was the proximate cause: wind lifted the shingles, rain entered, and the ceiling collapsed in one unbroken chain.

terms.definition: independent claims adjuster representing policyholders instead of insurance companies.
examples: The homeowner hired a public adjuster to press her fire claim, since that adjuster works for her rather than the insurer.

terms.definition: A guarantee that a public official will properly account for public funds and perform duties prescribed by law.
examples: The public official bond guarantees the treasurer will account properly for the town's funds.

terms.definition: that portion of the premium equal to expected losses void of insurance company expenses, premium taxes, contingencies, or profit margin.
examples: The pure premium covers expected losses alone, before commissions, taxes, or profit are added.

terms.definition: circumstance including possibility of loss or no loss but no possibility of gain.
examples: Fire is a pure risk: the building either burns or it does not, and there is no upside.

terms.definition: a person who meets the basic education, experience and continuing education requirements (these differ by line of business) of the Specific Qualification Standard for Statements of Actuarial Opinion, NAIC Property and Casualty Annual Statement, as set forth in the Qualification Standards for Actuaries Issuing Statements of Actuarial Opinion in the United States, promulgated by the American Academy of Actuaries, and is in good standing of the American Academy of Actuaries who has been approved as qualified for signing casualty loss reserve opinions by the Casualty Practice Council of the American Academy of Actuaries.
examples: Only a qualified actuary may sign the statement of actuarial opinion filed with the annual statement.

terms.definition: An employee whose expected permanent disability from a worker injury permanently precludes, or is likely to preclude, the employee from engaging in their usual occupation.
examples: Because his permanent restrictions ruled out his old trade, he was found a qualified injured worker eligible for retraining.

terms.definition: Under California workers' compensation, an evaluation performed by an independent physician certified to perform medical evaluations.
examples: The qualified medical evaluation resolved the dispute over whether the condition was work-related.

terms.definition: Under workers' compensation, a person trained to develop and implement a vocational rehabilitation plan; also known as a rehabilitation counselor.
examples: The qualified rehabilitation representative built a retraining plan and helped the worker enrol in the program.

terms.definition: Reinsurance in which the reinsurer accepts a share of the risk, sharing all losses and expenses as agreed.
examples: Under quota share reinsurance the reinsurer takes twenty-five percent of every policy in the book, premiums and losses alike.

terms.definition: Estimate of insurance cost based on applicant information.
examples: The quote came back at $1,850 a year, subject to inspection of the roof.

terms.definition: Coverage against loss of expense incurred, or income expected, due to reduced patronage from rain, hail, snow, or sleet.
examples: The festival organiser bought rain insurance to cover the ticket revenue lost if the weekend was washed out.

terms.definition: The price of insurance based on expected claim payouts and individual risk factors.
examples: The rate reflects both expected claims and factors like the driver's history and where the car is kept.

terms.definition: a refund of part or all of a premium payment.
examples: Offering a rebate of part of the premium to win the sale is prohibited in most states.

terms.definition: Restoring a lapsed policy to full force, possibly requiring insurability evidence.
examples: Reinstatement after the lapse required payment of the overdue premium and proof that his health had not changed.

terms.definition: a transaction between a primary insurer and another licensed (re) insurer where the reinsurer agrees to cover all or part of the losses and/or loss adjustment expenses of the primary insurer. The assumption is in exchange for a premium. Indemnification is on a proportional or non-proportional basis.
examples: Reinsurance let the insurer take on the large refinery risk by passing most of it to a reinsurer for a premium.

terms.definition: Claim amounts an insurer or pool recovers from reinsurers on claims meeting or exceeding the limits established in a reinsurance treaty.
examples: Reinsurance recoveries on that catastrophe amounted to $4 million once losses passed the treaty limit.

terms.definition: An insurer that reinsures the risks of another insurer or pool under a contract of reinsurance.
examples: The reinsurer never deals with the policyholder, only with the insurer whose risks it accepts.

terms.definition: insurance that is renewable for a limited number of successive terms by the policyholder and is not contingent upon medical examination.
examples: Renewable term insurance let him extend the coverage for another five years without a new medical exam.

terms.definition: The continuation of a coverage agreement or insurance contract beyond its original expiration date.
examples: At renewal the insurer offered the same coverage for another year at a slightly higher premium.

terms.definition: liability coverage for contents within a renter's residence. Coverage does not include the structure but does include any affixed items provided or changed by the renter.
examples: Renters insurance covered her furniture and laptop, but not the building itself.

terms.definition: the cost of replacing property without a reduction for depreciation due to normal wear and tear.
examples: Replacement cost pays what a new roof costs today, with no deduction for the old one's age.

terms.definition: Insurance providing that the insured will be paid the cost of replacing damaged property without deduction for depreciation.
examples: Replacement cost insurance paid the full price of new appliances rather than the depreciated value of the old ones.

terms.definition: Full cost to repair or replace damaged property with no depreciation deduction.
examples: Because the policy pays replacement value, the twelve-year-old furnace was replaced with a new equivalent unit.

terms.definition: The liability for losses on accidents or occurrences for which notice or a report of loss has been received.
examples: Reported loss reserves cover only those accidents the insurer already knows about.

terms.definition: Includes both expected payments for losses relating to insured events that have occurred and have been reported to the insurance company, but not yet paid.
examples: Reported losses include claims that have been notified and reserved but not yet paid.

terms.definition: A legal doctrine, meaning "the facts speak for themselves," presuming an insured's negligence when an injury occurs through a situation under its sole control that would not have occurred with due care.
examples: Res ipsa loquitur applied when a surgical sponge was left inside the patient, since that does not happen with due care.

terms.definition: A portion of the premium retained to pay future claims
examples: The insurer holds part of the premium as a reserve to pay claims that are still open.

terms.definition: reduction of reserve amounts for reinsurance ceded. Reductions may include the claim reserve and/or the unearned premium reserve.
examples: The ceding insurer took a reserve credit for the reinsurance, reducing both its claim and unearned premium reserves.

terms.definition: Unpaid claim liabilities comprised of case reserves and incurred but not reported reserves.
examples: Reserves on the balance sheet combine case reserves on known claims with an IBNR estimate for the rest.

terms.definition: the domicile location of a member as shown by his or her determination as a resident.
examples: The member's residence determines which plan rules and rates apply.

terms.definition: method devised for coverage of greater than average risk individuals who cannot obtain insurance through normal market channels.
examples: When no standard carrier would insure the coastal property, a residual market plan provided coverage.

terms.definition: The fund balance or surplus of uncommitted dollars belonging to a pool's members, usable at the discretion of its board of trustees.
examples: The pool's retained earnings gave the trustees a cushion to draw on in a bad claims year.

terms.definition: a mechanism of internal fund allocation for loss exposure used in place of or as a supplement to risk transfer to an insurance company.
examples: Rather than insure minor damage, the company chose retention and funded those small losses internally.

terms.definition: maximum amount of medical and hospital expense an insurer will carry on its own. The limit can be for an individual claim and/or for the insurers total claims, depending upon the terms of the reinsurance contract.
examples: The insurer's retention limit is $250,000 per claim, and reinsurance covers anything above that.

terms.definition: the portion of risk that a reinsurance company cedes or amount of insurance the company chooses not to retain.
examples: The reinsurer bought retrocession, passing part of what it had assumed to another reinsurer.

terms.definition: the process of determining the cost of an insurance policy based on the actual loss experience determined as an adjustment to the initial premium payment.
examples: Under retrospective rating the final premium was adjusted upward after a bad claims year.

terms.definition: An individual whose primary responsibility is assisting in the development of each injured worker's return-to-work plan.
examples: The return-to-work coordinator lined up the modified duties before the worker's release date.

terms.definition: An individual plan designed to assist an injured worker's successful return to work, including timeframes and schedules based on the injury and the worker's abilities.
examples: The return-to-work plan started him at four hours a day and built up to full shifts over six weeks.

terms.definition: An employer or insurer program that facilitates injured workers' return to safe and productive work as soon as physically possible.
examples: The employer's return-to-work program cut lost days by finding safe tasks for recovering workers.

terms.definition: Policy amendment adding or deleting coverage.
examples: A rider added earthquake coverage to the homeowners policy midterm.

terms.definition: Uncertainty as to the outcome of an event, or the measure of the combined probability and severity of potential harm from exposure to a hazard.
examples: The underwriter weighed the risk of a wildfire loss against the premium the property would generate.

terms.definition: The acceptance by an individual or organization of a level of risk identified as a potential consequence of a course of action.
examples: The board accepted the risk of minor theft losses rather than pay for coverage.

terms.definition: The process of determining the degree of threat posed by one or more hazards to one or more resources.
examples: The risk assessment ranked flooding as the plant's most serious threat and fire second.

terms.definition: ratio used to identify insurance companies that are poorly capitalized. Calculated by dividing the company's capital by the minimum amount of capital regulatory authorities have deemed necessary to support the insurance operations.
examples: An RBC ratio below the regulatory threshold flagged the insurer as poorly capitalized.

terms.definition: A classification of the risks associated with an incident, e.g. depending on industry type.
examples: Roofing contractors fall into a higher risk class than office employers.

terms.definition: The professional assessment of all loss potentials in an organization, leading to the establishment of a comprehensive loss-control program encompassing insurance, self-insurance, and assumed risk.
examples: Risk management reviewed every exposure and built a program mixing insurance, self-insurance, and loss prevention.

terms.definition: An electronic system used to perform and document claim and billing activities and to provide data and reports.
examples: The RMIS logged every payment and reserve change and generated the monthly claim reports.

terms.definition: A management-level person typically responsible for insurance programs and other activities that minimize losses from fire, accidents, and other events.
examples: The risk manager negotiated the renewal, ran the safety committee, and set the retention levels.

terms.definition: The process of minimizing accidental loss by anticipating and preventing unplanned events, encompassing worker safety, property conservation, and related elements.
examples: Risk prevention put machine guards, floor markings, and a lockout procedure in place before anyone was hurt.

terms.definition: a 1986 federal statute amending portions of the Product Liability Risk Retention Act of 1981 and enacted to make organization of Risk Retention Groups and Purchasing Groups more efficient.
examples: The Risk Retention Act made it easier for similar businesses to form their own group insurer across state lines.

terms.definition: group-owned insurer organized for the purpose of assuming and spreading the liability risks to its members.
examples: Twenty trucking firms formed a risk retention group to insure their own liability exposures.

terms.definition: The act of accepting a perceived risk that may expose others to a danger, whether voluntarily or involuntarily accepted.
examples: Risk-sharing among the member districts meant one large claim was funded by the whole group.

terms.definition: Coverage providing assistance for vehicle breakdowns or related issues.
examples: Road service covered the tow when the transmission failed on the highway.

terms.definition: The unlawful taking of property by violence, force, or intimidation.
examples: Taking the cash by threatening the clerk was robbery, not burglary.

terms.definition: The major act of omission or commission that resulted in loss, damage, or injury.
examples: The investigation found the root cause of loss was an unrepaired seal that had been flagged three months earlier.

terms.definition: The value of recovered property or the sale of partially damaged property.
examples: The insurer sold the damaged stock for salvage and credited $8,000 against the claim payment.

terms.definition: a method for insurance companies to access capital and hedge risks by converting policies into securities that can be sold in financial markets.
